docs.text: The Data Gateway section has complete examples of its configuration, its REST, MCP and WebSocket APIs and its UI; start with Getting started.

docs.title: Bulk Insert
docs.text:
This page shows how to insert many records at once with bulkInsert. Use it instead of Insert when you have a list of records to load, such as an import or a large dataset. The SQL shown is the one generated for MySQL.

bulkInsert receives an array of records and inserts them in chunks, with one statement per chunk instead of one statement per record. The size of the chunks depends on the connection, and you can lower it with the chunkSize option of orm.execute. This reduces the round trips between the application and the database, which makes inserting large volumes of data much faster and lightens the load on the database server.

docs.title: Bulk insert into one entity
docs.text:
Inserts a list of categories.

Lambda:

Categories.bulkInsert()

SQL Result:

INSERT INTO Categories(CategoryName,Description) VALUES ?

docs.title: Bulk insert with a related entity
docs.text:
Inserts a list of orders, each one with its details.

Lambda:

Orders.bulkInsert().include(p => p.details)

SQL Result:

-- the orders
INSERT INTO Orders(CustomerID,EmployeeID,OrderDate,RequiredDate,ShippedDate,ShipVia,Freight,ShipName,ShipAddress,ShipCity,ShipRegion,ShipPostalCode,ShipCountry) VALUES ?

-- the details of all the orders
INSERT INTO `Order Details`(OrderID,ProductID,UnitPrice,Quantity,Discount) VALUES ?

docs.title: Code example
docs.text:
Inserts two categories and prints the ids of the records inserted.

import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib'
import { Categories } from './domain/model' // model generated by `lambdaorm build`

(async () => {
    try {
        await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml')
        const categories = [
            { name: 'Beverages4', description: 'Soft drinks, coffees, teas, beers, and ales' },
            { name: 'Condiments4', description: 'Sweet and savory sauces, relishes, spreads, and seasonings' }
        ]
        const query = () => Categories.bulkInsert()
        // returns the ids of the records inserted
        const result = await orm.execute(query, categories)
        console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2))
    } catch (error: any) {
        console.error(error.stack)
    } finally {
        // releases the connections
        await orm.end()
    }
})()

docs.title: Delete
docs.text:
This page shows how to delete records: with a filter, by primary key, all the records of an entity, and together with related entities. The SQL shown is the one generated for MySQL.

delete returns the number of affected rows: 0 means that no row matched the filter.

const count = await orm.execute('Categories.delete().filter(p => p.id == id)', { id: 9 }) // 1

docs.title: Delete with a filter
docs.text:
Deletes the details of an order.

Lambda:

Orders.details.delete().filter(p => p.orderId === id)

SQL Result:

DELETE o FROM `Order Details` AS o WHERE o.OrderID = ?

docs.title: Delete by primary key
docs.text:
When delete() has no filter, it filters by the primary key, whose value is taken from the data passed. The primary key of the order details is made of orderId and productId:

Lambda:

Orders.details.delete()

SQL Result:

DELETE o FROM `Order Details` AS o WHERE (o.OrderID = ? AND o.ProductID = ?)

docs.title: Delete all the records
docs.text:
To delete all the records of an entity, use deleteAll instead of delete. This prevents deleting all the records by mistake.

Lambda:

Orders.details.deleteAll()

SQL Result:

DELETE FROM `Order Details`

docs.title: Delete an entity and its related entities
docs.text:
Deletes an order and its details. The order is filtered by its primary key, and each detail sent by its own primary key. The details are deleted first, and then the order.

Lambda:

Orders.delete().include(p => p.details)

SQL Result:

-- the order
DELETE o FROM Orders AS o WHERE o.OrderID = ?

-- each detail sent
DELETE o1 FROM `Order Details` AS o1 WHERE (o1.OrderID = ? AND o1.ProductID = ?)

docs.title: Code example
docs.text:
Deletes an order with its details and prints the number of orders deleted.

import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib'
import { Orders } from './domain/model' // model generated by `lambdaorm build`

(async () => {
    try {
        await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml')
        const order = {
            id: 1,
            customerId: 'ALFKI',
            employeeId: 6,
            orderDate: '1997-08-24T22:00:00.000Z',
            requiredDate: '1997-09-21T22:00:00.000Z',
            shippedDate: '1997-09-01T22:00:00.000Z',
            shipViaId: 1,
            freight: '29.4600',
            name: 'Alfreds Futterkiste',
            address: 'Obere Str. 57',
            city: 'Berlin',
            region: null,
            postalCode: '12209',
            country: 'Germany',
            details: [
                {
                    orderId: 1,
                    productId: 28,
                    unitPrice: '45.6000',
                    quantity: '15.0000',
                    discount: '0.0000'
                },
                {
                    orderId: 1,
                    productId: 39,
                    unitPrice: '18.0000',
                    quantity: '21.0000',
                    discount: '0.0000'
                }
            ]
        }
        const query = () => Orders.delete().include(p => p.details)
        // returns the number of orders deleted
        const count = await orm.execute(query, order)
        console.log(count)
    } catch (error: any) {
        console.error(error.stack)
    } finally {
        // releases the connections
        await orm.end()
    }
})()

docs.title: Lambda expressions
docs.text:
This page summarizes the building blocks of a λORM query: the methods you chain on an entity, and the operators and functions you can use inside the lambdas. Use it as a quick reference; each method links to the page with its examples.

Queries are lambda expressions written in the programming language itself. They refer to the entities and properties of the domain, so they are independent of the database language and of how the data is stored.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The following query reads the products whose name starts with "A", with the name of their category, sorted by category (ascending) and product (descending), and returns the first page of 10 records:

Products
    .filter(p => upper(substr(p.name, 1, 1)) == "A")
    .map(p => ({ category: p.category.name, product: p.name }))
    .sort(p => [p.category, desc(p.product)])
    .page(1, 10)

On Oracle, λORM translates it into:

SELECT c.CategoryName AS "category", p.ProductName AS "product"
FROM Products p
INNER JOIN Categories c ON c.CategoryID = p.CategoryID
WHERE UPPER(SUBSTR(p.ProductName,1,1)) = 'A'
ORDER BY "category" asc, "product" desc
OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 10 ROWS ONLY

The same query runs on any other engine: on MySQL, for example, the pagination becomes LIMIT 0,10.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Queries are written in the same programming language as the application.
  • There is no new language to learn.
  • Expressions are easy to write and to read.
  • The IDE's IntelliSense helps you write the expressions.
  • Syntax errors are caught while you write.

docs.title: Query methods
docs.text:
Method Description SQL equivalent Examples filter Filters the records. WHERE Select having Filters the groups. HAVING Grouping map Specifies the properties to return. SELECT Select distinct Specifies the properties to return, removing duplicate records. SELECT DISTINCT Select first Returns the first record. SELECT + ORDER BY + LIMIT Select last Returns the last record. SELECT + ORDER BY DESC + LIMIT Select sort Specifies the order of the records. ORDER BY Select page Paginates the records. LIMIT / OFFSET (depends on the dialect) Select include Loads the records of related entities. Include insert Inserts a record. INSERT Insert upsert Inserts a record, or updates it if one with the same primary key exists. INSERT … ON CONFLICT / MERGE Insert bulkInsert Inserts many records at once. INSERT Bulk Insert update Updates records; it always has a filter. UPDATE with WHERE Update updateAll Updates all the records of an entity. UPDATE without WHERE Update delete Deletes records; it always has a filter. DELETE with WHERE Delete deleteAll Deletes all the records of an entity. DELETE without WHERE Delete
  • There is no method for joins: an INNER JOIN is deduced when the query navigates a relation, as in p.category.name (see Join).
  • There is no method for GROUP BY: it is deduced when an aggregate function is used (see Grouping).

docs.title: Operators
docs.text:
The operators are the same as in JavaScript.

Category Operators More info Arithmetic -, +, *, /, **, //, % Numeric Bitwise ~, &, \|, ^, <<, >> Bitwise Comparison ==, ===, !=, !==, >, <, >=, <= Comparison Logical !, &&, \|\| Logical Array []

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
Category Functions More info Numeric abs, ceil, cos, exp, ln, log, remainder, round, sign, sin, tan, trunc… Numeric String chr, lower, lpad, ltrim, replace, rpad, rtrim, substr, trim, upper, concat… String Datetime curTime, today, now, time, date, dateTime, year, month, day, weekday, hours… Datetime Convert toString, toJson, toNumber String Nullable nvl, nvl2, isNull, isNotNull Nullable General as, distinct Sort asc, desc Sort Condition between, includes Comparison Group avg, count, first, last, max, min, sum Group Metadata user, source

See Operators & Functions for the full reference.

docs.title: Grouping
docs.text:
This page shows how to group records and compute aggregates (sums, counts, maximums…), and how to filter the groups with having. The SQL shown is the one generated for MySQL.

You do not declare the grouping: λORM deduces it when the query uses an aggregate function. The records are grouped by the properties returned that are not inside an aggregate function.

docs.title: Aggregate functions
docs.text: Function Description avg Calculates the average of the values in a group. count Counts the records in a group. first Returns the first value in a group. last Returns the last value in a group. max Calculates the maximum. min Calculates the minimum. sum Calculates the sum.

docs.title: Sum with filter and sort
docs.text:
Reads, for the orders of a customer, the order date and the total (sum of quantity × unit price), sorted by total in descending order. The records are grouped by order, the only property returned that is not an aggregate.

Lambda:

Orders.details
    .filter(p => p.order.customer.name == customerName)
    .map(p => ({ order: p.order.orderDate, total: sum(p.quantity * p.unitPrice) }))
    .sort(p => desc(p.total))

SQL Result:

SELECT o1.OrderDate AS `order`, SUM((o.Quantity * o.UnitPrice)) AS total
FROM `Order Details` o
INNER JOIN Orders o1 ON o1.OrderID = o.OrderID
INNER JOIN Customers c ON c.CustomerID = o1.CustomerID
WHERE c.CompanyName = ?
GROUP BY o1.OrderDate
ORDER BY total desc

docs.title: Grouping and having
docs.text:
Reads the highest price of each category, considering the products with a price greater than 5 whose supplier is from a given country, or with fewer than 3 units in stock. Only the categories whose highest price is greater than 50 are returned, sorted by that price in descending order.

filter is applied to the records before grouping (WHERE); having is applied to the groups (HAVING).

Lambda:

Products
    .filter(p => (p.price > 5 && p.supplier.country == country) || (p.inStock < 3))
    .having(p => max(p.price) > 50)
    .map(p => ({ category: p.category.name, largestPrice: max(p.price) }))
    .sort(p => desc(p.largestPrice))

SQL Result:

SELECT c.CategoryName AS category, MAX(p.UnitPrice) AS largestPrice
FROM Products p
INNER JOIN Suppliers s ON s.SupplierID = p.SupplierID
INNER JOIN Categories c ON c.CategoryID = p.CategoryID
WHERE ((p.UnitPrice > 5 AND s.Country = ?) OR p.UnitsInStock < 3)
GROUP BY c.CategoryName
HAVING MAX(p.UnitPrice) > 50
ORDER BY largestPrice desc

docs.title: Code example
docs.text:
import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib'
import { Products } from './domain/model' // model generated by `lambdaorm build`

(async () => {
    try {
        await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml')
        // highest price per category, for the categories whose highest price is greater than 50
        const query = (country: string) => Products
            .filter(p => (p.price > 5 && p.supplier.country == country) || (p.inStock < 3))
            .having(p => max(p.price) > 50)
            .map(p => ({ category: p.category.name, largestPrice: max(p.price) }))
            .sort(p => desc(p.largestPrice))
        const result = await orm.execute(query, { country: 'USA' })
        console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2))
    } catch (error: any) {
        console.error(error.stack)
    } finally {
        // releases the connections
        await orm.end()
    }
})()

docs.title: Include
docs.text:
This page shows how to load related entities together with the main entity, using the include method. Use it when the result must contain an object with its relations (an order with its customer and its details), or when the related entity is in another source.

include works with every type of relation (oneToMany, manyToOne and oneToOne, see relations). In λORM terms, a oneToMany relation points to one record (each order has one customer) and a manyToOne relation is a collection (each order has many details). Inside an include you can also filter the related records and choose their properties.

For each include, λORM runs one statement that reads all the related records needed, and then assembles the objects in memory. This avoids running one statement per record, which considerably improves performance. To link the records, λORM adds the keys it needs to the statements (__customerId, LambdaOrmParentId…); they are removed from the result.

Includes can be used in selects, inserts, upserts, updates, deletes and bulk inserts. The SQL shown on this page is the one generated for MySQL.

docs.title: Include a oneToMany relation
docs.text:
Reads an order and its customer.

Lambda:

Orders.filter(p => p.id == id).include(p => p.customer)

SQL Result:

-- the order
SELECT o.OrderID AS id, o.CustomerID AS customerId, o.EmployeeID AS employeeId, o.OrderDate AS orderDate,
  o.RequiredDate AS requiredDate, o.ShippedDate AS shippedDate, o.ShipVia AS shipViaId, o.Freight AS freight,
  o.ShipName AS name, o.ShipAddress AS address, o.ShipCity AS city, o.ShipRegion AS region,
  o.ShipPostalCode AS postalCode, o.ShipCountry AS country, o.CustomerID AS `__customerId`
FROM Orders o
WHERE o.OrderID = ?

-- the customers of the orders read above
SELECT c.CustomerID AS id, c.CompanyName AS name, c.ContactName AS contact, c.ContactTitle AS phone,
  c.Address AS address, c.City AS city, c.Region AS region, c.PostalCode AS postalCode, c.Country AS country,
  c.CustomerID AS LambdaOrmParentId
FROM Customers c
WHERE c.CustomerID IN (?)

Data Result:

[
  {
    "id": 10248,
    "customerId": "VINET",
    "employeeId": 5,
    "orderDate": "1996-07-03T22:00:00.000Z",

]

docs.title: Include manyToOne and oneToMany relations
docs.text:
Reads an order with its details and its customer. To include several relations, return them in an array.

Lambda:

Orders.filter(p => p.id == id).include(p => [p.details, p.customer])

SQL Result:

-- the order
SELECT o.OrderID AS id, o.CustomerID AS customerId, o.EmployeeID AS employeeId, o.OrderDate AS orderDate,
  o.RequiredDate AS requiredDate, o.ShippedDate AS shippedDate, o.ShipVia AS shipViaId, o.Freight AS freight,
  o.ShipName AS name, o.ShipAddress AS address, o.ShipCity AS city, o.ShipRegion AS region,
  o.ShipPostalCode AS postalCode, o.ShipCountry AS country, o.OrderID AS `__id`, o.CustomerID AS `__customerId`
FROM Orders o
WHERE o.OrderID = ?

-- the details of the orders read above
SELECT o1.OrderID AS orderId, o1.ProductID AS productId, o1.UnitPrice AS unitPrice, o1.Quantity AS quantity,
  o1.Discount AS discount, o1.OrderID AS LambdaOrmParentId
FROM `Order Details` o1
WHERE o1.OrderID IN (?)

-- the customers of the orders read above

  c.Address AS address, c.City AS city, c.Region AS region, c.PostalCode AS postalCode, c.Country AS country,
  c.CustomerID AS LambdaOrmParentId

    "shippedDate": "1996-07-15T22:00:00.000Z",

docs.title: Nested includes
docs.text:
An included relation can include its own relations. This example reads an order with its customer and its details; for each detail it reads the product, and for each product its category.

Lambda:

Orders
    .filter(p => p.id == id)
    .include(p => [p.details.include(q => q.product.include(r => r.category)), p.customer])

SQL Result:

-- the order
SELECT o.OrderID AS id, o.CustomerID AS customerId, o.EmployeeID AS employeeId, o.OrderDate AS orderDate,
  o.RequiredDate AS requiredDate, o.ShippedDate AS shippedDate, o.ShipVia AS shipViaId, o.Freight AS freight,
  o.ShipName AS name, o.ShipAddress AS address, o.ShipCity AS city, o.ShipRegion AS region,
  o.ShipPostalCode AS postalCode, o.ShipCountry AS country, o.OrderID AS `__id`, o.CustomerID AS `__customerId`

docs.title: Include only some properties
docs.text:
You can choose the properties to return both for the main entity and for each included entity, so that the query returns only the data you need. This example reads the date of an order; the name and full address of its customer; the quantity and unit price of its details; the name of each product and the name of its category.

Lambda:

Orders.filter(p => p.id === id)
    .include(p => [
        // name of the customer and full address
        p.customer.map(p => ({
            name: p.name,
            address: concat(p.address, ', ', p.city, ' (', p.postalCode, ')  ', p.country)
        })),
        // quantity and unit price of the details, with the name of the product and of its category
        p.details.include(p => p.product
                .include(p => p.category.map(p => p.name))
                .map(p => p.name))
            .map(p => [p.quantity, p.unitPrice])
    ])
    // date of the order
    .map(p => p.orderDate)

SQL Result:

-- the order
SELECT o.OrderDate AS orderDate, o.CustomerID AS `__customerId`, o.OrderID AS `__id`
FROM Orders o
WHERE o.OrderID = ?

-- the customers of the orders
SELECT c.CompanyName AS name,
  CONCAT(CONCAT(CONCAT(CONCAT(CONCAT(CONCAT(c.Address,', '),c.City),' ('),c.PostalCode),')  '),c.Country) AS address,
  c.CustomerID AS LambdaOrmParentId
FROM Customers c
WHERE c.CustomerID IN (?)

-- the details of the orders
SELECT o1.Quantity AS quantity, o1.UnitPrice AS unitPrice, o1.ProductID AS `__productId`, o1.OrderID AS LambdaOrmParentId
FROM `Order Details` o1
WHERE o1.OrderID IN (?)

-- the products of the details
SELECT p.ProductName AS name, p.CategoryID AS `__categoryId`, p.ProductID AS LambdaOrmParentId
FROM Products p
WHERE p.ProductID IN (?)

-- the categories of the products
SELECT c1.CategoryName AS name, c1.CategoryID AS LambdaOrmParentId
FROM Categories c1
WHERE c1.CategoryID IN (?)

docs.title: Relations in another source
docs.text:
The related entity can be in another source (another database or schema) of the stage. Since each include runs as a separate statement, include works across sources at any depth:

// Orders and OrderLines in one source, Products and Categories in another
Orders.filter(p => p.id == id).include(p => p.lines.include(l => l.product.include(q => q.category)))

docs.title: Filter by a field of a relation in another source
docs.text:
A filter can also use a property of a relation whose entity is in another source. The other source is queried first, and the keys found are then used to filter with in:

Lambda:

// OrderLines (source "sales") filtered by the name of its product (source "catalog")
OrderLines.filter(p => p.product.name == name && p.orderId == orderId)

Executed as:

// 1. on the source of Products
Products.filter(p => p.name == name)
// 2. on the source of OrderLines, with the ids found in 1
OrderLines.filter(p => in(p.productId, ids) && p.orderId == orderId)

Each comparison is replaced on its own, so &&, || and ! keep their meaning.

  • It can be combined with other conditions, also with ||: OrderLines.filter(p => p.orderId == orderId && (p.product.name == name || p.quantity > 100)).
  • When the other source has no match, the query returns no rows.
  • Only one level of relation is supported (p.product.name, not p.product.category.name).
  • The other side of each comparison must be a value (a literal or a variable). Comparing with a property, as in p.product.name == p.description, fails with an error saying that the relation is in another source.

docs.title: Code example
docs.text:
The query of Include only some properties, run from Node with @lambdaorm/lib:

import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib'
import { Orders } from './domain/model' // model generated by `lambdaorm build`

(async () => {
    try {
        await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml')
        const query = (id: number) => Orders
            .filter(p => p.id === id)
            .include(p => [
                p.customer.map(p => ({
                    name: p.name,
                    address: concat(p.address, ', ', p.city, ' (', p.postalCode, ')  ', p.country)
                })),
                p.details.include(p => p.product
                        .include(p => p.category.map(p => p.name))
                        .map(p => p.name))
                    .map(p => [p.quantity, p.unitPrice])
            ])
            .map(p => p.orderDate)
        const result = await orm.execute(query, { id: 10248 })
        console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2))
    } catch (error: any) {
        console.error(error.stack)
    } finally {
        // releases the connections
        await orm.end()
    }
})()

docs.title: Insert
docs.text:
This page shows how to insert records: with all the properties of the entity or only some of them, together with related entities (include), and how to insert or update in one step (upsert). To insert many records at once, see Bulk Insert. The SQL shown is the one generated for MySQL, unless stated otherwise.

A query is based on both the expression and the schema. If you do not specify the properties to insert, all the properties of the entity are inserted. How each property is stored in each source (table and column names) is resolved by the mapping of that source in the schema.

docs.title: Insert all the properties
docs.text:
When the properties are not specified, the data passed must be an object with the properties of the entity.

Lambda:

Categories.insert()

SQL Result:

INSERT INTO Categories(CategoryName,Description) VALUES(?,?)

The primary key id is not inserted because it is auto-increment: the database generates it.

docs.title: Insert some properties
docs.text:
Only the properties specified are inserted. Here, name is a variable of the data passed to the query.

Lambda:

Categories.insert({ name: name })

SQL Result:

INSERT INTO Categories(CategoryName) VALUES(?)

docs.title: Insert with include
docs.text:
To insert an object together with its related objects, include the relation. This example inserts an order and its details; the key of the new order is assigned to each detail.

Lambda:

Orders.insert().include(p => p.details)

SQL Result:

-- the order
INSERT INTO Orders(CustomerID,EmployeeID,OrderDate,RequiredDate,ShippedDate,ShipVia,Freight,ShipName,ShipAddress,ShipCity,ShipRegion,ShipPostalCode,ShipCountry)
VALUES(?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?)

-- each detail of the order
INSERT INTO `Order Details`(OrderID,ProductID,UnitPrice,Quantity,Discount)
VALUES(?,?,?,?,?)

docs.title: Upsert
docs.text:
upsert() inserts the record or, if a record with the same primary key already exists, updates it. It is written like an insert: upsert() with all the properties, or with the properties specified. The entity needs a primary key, and the data must include it (so an auto-increment key is of little use here).

Lambda:

// inserts the country, or updates it when one with the same iso3 exists
Countries.upsert()

await orm.execute('Countries.upsert()', { iso3: 'ARG', name: 'Argentine' }) // inserted
await orm.execute('Countries.upsert()', { iso3: 'ARG', name: 'Argentina' }) // updated: the same row

SQL Result:

-- MySQL / MariaDB
INSERT INTO Countries(iso3,name) VALUES(?,?) ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE name = VALUES(name)

-- PostgreSQL
INSERT INTO Countries(iso3,name) VALUES($1,$2)
ON CONFLICT (iso3) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name

-- SQL Server
MERGE INTO Countries WITH (HOLDLOCK) AS t
USING (SELECT 1 AS x) AS s
ON t.iso3 = @iso3
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET name = @name
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (iso3,name) VALUES (@iso3,@name);

-- Oracle
MERGE INTO Countries t
USING (SELECT 1 FROM DUAL) s
ON (t.iso3 = :iso3)
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET name = :name
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (iso3,name) VALUES (:iso3,:name)

Upsert is supported on PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server and Oracle (these two with MERGE, from @lambdaorm/lib 3.5.0).

Warning

On MongoDB, upsert fails with a "not supported yet" error. SQLite (SQL.js) does not support it either.

When the key is generated (auto-increment) and not sent, the upsert inserts. On SQL Server the identity column is never inserted (the database generates it) and OUTPUT INSERTED returns it; Oracle's MERGE cannot return values, so it returns the key that was sent.

Upsert is also what an update with include of a composite relation uses to save the children.

docs.title: Code example
docs.text:
Inserts an order with two details and prints the id of the new order.

import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib'
import { Orders } from './domain/model' // model generated by `lambdaorm build`

(async () => {
    try {
        await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml')
        const order = {
            customerId: 'VINET',
            employeeId: 5,
            orderDate: '1996-07-03T22:00:00.000Z',
            requiredDate: '1996-07-31T22:00:00.000Z',
            shippedDate: '1996-07-15T22:00:00.000Z',
            shipViaId: 3,
            freight: 32.38,
            name: 'Vins et alcools Chevalier',
            address: '59 rue de l-Abbaye',
            city: 'Reims',
            postalCode: '51100',
            country: 'France',
            // orderId is assigned from the new order
            details: [
                { productId: 11, unitPrice: 14, quantity: 12, discount: 10 },
                { productId: 42, unitPrice: 9.8, quantity: 10, discount: 10 }
            ]
        }
        const query = () => Orders.insert().include(p => p.details)
        // returns the id of the order created
        const result = await orm.execute(query, order)
        console.log(JSON.stringify(result))
    } catch (error: any) {
        console.error(error.stack)
    } finally {
        // releases the connections
        await orm.end()
    }
})()

docs.title: Join
docs.text:
This page shows how λORM reads properties of related entities. There is no join method: when a query uses a property through a relation, such as p.category.name, λORM adds the join that the relation defines in the schema. The SQL shown is the one generated for MySQL.

Note

A join needs both entities in the same source. To read related entities that are in another source, use Include; to filter by a property of a relation in another source, see Filter by a field of a relation in another source.

docs.title: Simple join
docs.text:
Reads the name of each product and the name of its category, through the category relation.

Lambda:

Products.map(p => ({ name: p.name, category: p.category.name }))

SQL Result:

SELECT p.ProductName AS name, c.CategoryName AS category
FROM Products p
INNER JOIN Categories c ON c.CategoryID = p.CategoryID

docs.title: Join with distinct and sort
docs.text:
Reads the distinct combinations of quantity per unit and category name, sorted by category.

Lambda:

Products
    .distinct(p => ({ quantity: p.quantity, category: p.category.name }))
    .sort(p => p.category)

SQL Result:

SELECT DISTINCT p.QuantityPerUnit AS quantity, c.CategoryName AS category
FROM Products p
INNER JOIN Categories c ON c.CategoryID = p.CategoryID
ORDER BY category asc

docs.title: Join with filter
docs.text:
Reads the name and category of the products with a price greater than 10.

Lambda:

Products
    .filter(p => p.price > 10)
    .map(p => ({ name: p.name, category: p.category.name }))

SQL Result:

SELECT p.ProductName AS name, c.CategoryName AS category
FROM Products p
INNER JOIN Categories c ON c.CategoryID = p.CategoryID
WHERE p.UnitPrice > 10

docs.title: Join and pagination
docs.text:
Reads the name and category of the products with a price greater than 10, sorted by category, and returns the first page of 10 records.

Lambda:

Products
    .filter(p => p.price > 10)
    .map(p => ({ name: p.name, category: p.category.name }))
    .sort(p => p.category)
    .page(1, 10)

SQL Result:

SELECT p.ProductName AS name, c.CategoryName AS category
FROM Products p
INNER JOIN Categories c ON c.CategoryID = p.CategoryID
WHERE p.UnitPrice > 10
ORDER BY category asc
LIMIT 0,10

docs.title: Multiple joins and grouping
docs.text:
Reads, for the orders of a customer, the order date and the total (sum of quantity × unit price of its details), sorted by total in descending order. The query starts from the order details (Orders.details) and goes through two relations: order, and from the order, customer. Because sum is an aggregate function, λORM also groups by the order date (see Grouping).

Lambda:

Orders.details
    .filter(p => p.order.customer.name == customerName)
    .map(p => ({ order: p.order.orderDate, total: sum(p.quantity * p.unitPrice) }))
    .sort(p => desc(p.total))

SQL Result:

SELECT o1.OrderDate AS `order`, SUM((o.Quantity * o.UnitPrice)) AS total
FROM `Order Details` o
INNER JOIN Orders o1 ON o1.OrderID = o.OrderID
INNER JOIN Customers c ON c.CustomerID = o1.CustomerID
WHERE c.CompanyName = ?
GROUP BY o1.OrderDate
ORDER BY total desc

docs.title: Code example
docs.text:
import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib'
import { Orders } from './domain/model' // model generated by `lambdaorm build`

(async () => {
    try {
        await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml')
        const query = (customerName: string) => Orders.details
            .filter(p => p.order.customer.name == customerName)
            .map(p => ({ order: p.order.orderDate, total: sum(p.quantity * p.unitPrice) }))
            .sort(p => desc(p.total))
        const result = await orm.execute(query, { customerName: 'Vins et alcools Chevalier' }, { stage: 'MySQL' })
        console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2))
    } catch (error: any) {
        console.error(error.stack)
    } finally {
        await orm.end()
    }
})()

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
This page describes the methods that analyse a query without running it: the parameters it needs, the shape of its result, the constraints that apply, its analysed tree and the statements it would execute. Use them to validate a query, to build a form or a type for its data, or to see the SQL that λORM generates.

These methods do not access the database, so the connections are not needed: you can call orm.init(schema, false) to load the schema without connecting.

Method Description orm.parameters(query) The variables the query uses (which go in data), with their types. orm.model(query) The properties of the result, with their types. orm.constraints(query) The constraints that apply to the entities of the query. orm.metadata(query) The analysed tree of the query: each statement with its entity, columns, parameters and constraints. orm.plan(query, options?) How the query is executed: the dialect, the source and the statement of each part. options.stage selects the stage. orm.normalize(query) The query in its complete form, for example with the properties of map made explicit.

The query can be a lambda function or a string. The same information is available from the CLI (lambdaorm parameters, model, constraints, metadata, plan) and from the Data Gateway (POST /parameters, /model, /constraints, /metadata, /plan).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib'
import { Orders } from './domain/model' // model generated by `lambdaorm build`

(async () => {
    try {
        // load the schema without connecting to the databases
        await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml', false)
        const query = (id: number) => Orders
            .filter(p => p.id === id)
            .include(p => p.details)
            .map(p => ({ name: p.orderDate, customer: p.customer.name }))

        console.log(JSON.stringify(orm.parameters(query), null, 2))
        console.log(JSON.stringify(orm.model(query), null, 2))
        console.log(JSON.stringify(orm.constraints(query), null, 2))
        console.log(JSON.stringify(orm.metadata(query), null, 2))
        console.log(JSON.stringify(orm.plan(query, { stage: 'MySQL' }), null, 2))
    } catch (error: any) {
        console.error(error)
    } finally {
        await orm.end()
    }
})()

docs.title: Query Language
docs.text:
This page introduces the λORM query language: what a query looks like, the kinds of queries there are and where each one is documented.

λORM queries are written as JavaScript lambda expressions over the entities of the domain. You can write them as TypeScript/JavaScript code, navigating the entities of the model, or send them as a string (for example from the CLI or to the Data Gateway).

λORM translates each query into the language of the database engine of each source (SQL for MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle and SQLite, or MongoDB queries).

docs.title: DQL
docs.text:
DQL (Data Query Language) queries retrieve data. They can be as simple as reading all the records of an entity, or they can filter, sort, group and paginate the records, compute values from them and load related entities.

See: Select, Join, Grouping, Include

docs.title: DML
docs.text:
DML (Data Manipulation Language) queries change data. They include the following operations:

  • insert: adds new records to an entity (also bulkInsert and upsert).
  • update: modifies existing records.
  • delete: removes records.

See: Insert, Bulk Insert, Update, Delete

docs.title: DDL
docs.text:
DDL (Data Definition Language) statements create, modify and drop database structures and related objects:

  • CREATE: creates new objects in the database, such as tables and indexes.
  • ALTER: modifies the structure of existing objects, for example adding, changing or removing the columns of a table.
  • DROP: deletes objects from the database.

You do not write DDL queries: λORM generates and runs them when you use the schema synchronization commands.

See: Push, Pull, Fetch, Introspect, Incorporate

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The following query reads the countries of a region, with their states whose name starts with "F". It returns the name, subregion and position of each country, 3 countries per page:

Countries
    .filter(p => p.region == region)
    .map(p => [p.name, p.subregion, p.latitude, p.longitude]) // properties of the country
    .include(p => p.states.filter(p => substr(p.name, 1, 1) == "F") // states starting with 'F'
        .map(p => [p.name, p.latitude, p.longitude])
    )
    .page(1, 3) // first page, 3 countries per page

In this schema, Countries is in a MySQL source and States in a PostgreSQL source (see Stage with multiple sources). λORM runs one statement per source:

-- MySQL: the countries of the region, first page of 3 records
SELECT c.name AS name, c.subregion AS subregion, c.latitude AS latitude, c.longitude AS longitude, c.iso3 AS `__iso3`
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.region = ?
ORDER BY c.name asc
LIMIT 0,3

-- PostgreSQL: the states starting with 'F' of the countries read above
SELECT s.NAME AS "name", s.LATITUDE AS "latitude", s.LONGITUDE AS "longitude", s.COUNTRY_CODE AS "LambdaOrmParentId"
FROM TBL_STATES s
WHERE SUBSTR(s.NAME,1,1) = 'F'
  AND s.COUNTRY_CODE IN (?)

The states are then attached to their country in memory, so each country of the result has a states array.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Queries are written in the same programming language as the application.
  • There is no new language to learn.
  • Queries are easy to write and to read.
  • The IDE's IntelliSense helps you write the expressions.
  • Syntax errors are caught while you write.

docs.title: Select
docs.text:
This page shows how to read records: all the properties of an entity or only some of them, the first or last record, distinct values and pagination. The SQL shown is the one generated for MySQL.

Every query is based on the schema, from which λORM knows the properties of each entity, its primary key, indexes, relations and constraints. That is why, to read all the properties of an entity, you do not need to list them.

docs.title: All the properties of an entity
docs.text:
Reads all the properties of all the products.

Lambda:

Products

SQL Result:

SELECT
    p.ProductID AS id,
    p.ProductName AS name,
    p.SupplierID AS supplierId,
    p.CategoryID AS categoryId,
    p.QuantityPerUnit AS quantity,
    p.UnitPrice AS price,
    p.UnitsInStock AS inStock,
    p.UnitsOnOrder AS onOrder,
    p.ReorderLevel AS reorderLevel,
    p.Discontinued AS discontinued
FROM Products p

docs.title: One property
docs.text:
Reads only the name of each product.

Lambda:

Products.map(p => p.name)

SQL Result:

SELECT p.ProductName AS name FROM Products p

docs.title: First
docs.text:
Reads the first product, ordered by its primary key.

Lambda:

Products.first()

SQL Result:

SELECT
    p.ProductID AS id,
    p.ProductName AS name,
    p.SupplierID AS supplierId,
    p.CategoryID AS categoryId,
    p.QuantityPerUnit AS quantity,
    p.UnitPrice AS price,
    p.UnitsInStock AS inStock,
    p.UnitsOnOrder AS onOrder,
    p.ReorderLevel AS reorderLevel,
    p.Discontinued AS discontinued
FROM Products p
ORDER BY p.ProductID asc
LIMIT 0,1

first can also receive the properties to return, as map does: Products.first(p => ({ name: p.name, price: p.price })). In that case the records are ordered by the first property returned.

docs.title: Last
docs.text:
Reads the last product, ordered by its primary key.

Lambda:

Products.last()

SQL Result:

SELECT
    p.ProductID AS id,
    p.ProductName AS name,
    p.SupplierID AS supplierId,
    p.CategoryID AS categoryId,
    p.QuantityPerUnit AS quantity,
    p.UnitPrice AS price,
    p.UnitsInStock AS inStock,
    p.UnitsOnOrder AS onOrder,
    p.ReorderLevel AS reorderLevel,
    p.Discontinued AS discontinued
FROM Products p
ORDER BY p.ProductID desc
LIMIT 0,1

docs.title: Distinct
docs.text:
Reads the distinct combinations of quantity per unit and category name, sorted by category. The category name comes from the category relation, so λORM adds the join (see Join).

Lambda:

Products
    .distinct(p => ({ quantity: p.quantity, category: p.category.name }))
    .sort(p => p.category)

SQL Result:

SELECT DISTINCT p.QuantityPerUnit AS quantity, c.CategoryName AS category
FROM Products p
INNER JOIN Categories c ON c.CategoryID = p.CategoryID
ORDER BY category asc

docs.title: Pagination
docs.text:
Reads the name and category of the products with a price greater than 10, sorted by category, and returns the first page of 10 records.

Lambda:

Products
    .filter(p => p.price > 10)
    .map(p => ({ name: p.name, category: p.category.name }))
    .sort(p => p.category)
    .page(1, 10)

SQL Result:

SELECT p.ProductName AS name, c.CategoryName AS category
FROM Products p
INNER JOIN Categories c ON c.CategoryID = p.CategoryID
WHERE p.UnitPrice > 10
ORDER BY category asc
LIMIT 0,10

page(page, records) receives the page number (starting at 1) and the number of records per page. How the page is expressed depends on the dialect: LIMIT on MySQL, OFFSET … FETCH NEXT … ROWS ONLY on Oracle, and so on.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: The same query, with the minimum price as a parameter (maxPrice), run in three ways.

docs.title: Node
docs.text:
With the library @lambdaorm/lib:

import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib'
import { Products } from './domain/model' // model generated by `lambdaorm build`

(async () => {
    try {
        await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml')
        // products with a price greater than maxPrice, with their category, first page of 10
        const query = (maxPrice: number) => Products
            .filter(p => p.price > maxPrice)
            .map(p => ({ name: p.name, category: p.category.name }))
            .sort(p => p.category)
            .page(1, 10)
        const result = await orm.execute(query, { maxPrice: 10 })
        console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2))
    } catch (error: any) {
        console.error(error.stack)
    } finally {
        // releases the connections
        await orm.end()
    }
})()

docs.title: Data Gateway
docs.text:
Through the REST API of the Data Gateway:

curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/execute?format=beautiful" -H "X-Api-Key: $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"query": "Products.filter(p=>p.price>maxPrice).map(p=>({name:p.name,category:p.category.name})).sort(p=>p.category).page(1,10)", "data": {"maxPrice": 10}}'

docs.title: Update
docs.text:
This page shows how to update records: all the properties or only some of them, with a filter or for all the records, together with related entities, and how to save a whole aggregate (a parent with its composite children). The SQL shown is the one generated for MySQL, unless stated otherwise.

A query is based on both the expression and the schema. If you do not specify the properties to update, all the properties of the entity are updated. How each property is stored in each source (table and column names) is resolved by the mapping of that source in the schema.

docs.title: Result: affected rows
docs.text:
update returns the number of affected rows (as delete does). 0 means that no row matched the filter, which is useful to answer "not found" or to detect a conflict with an optimistic lock:

const query = 'Orders.update(p => ({ status: status, version: version + 1 })).filter(p => p.id == id && p.version == version)'
const first = await orm.execute(query, { id: orderId, status: 'sent', version: 1 })     // 1
const second = await orm.execute(query, { id: orderId, status: 'accepted', version: 1 }) // 0: the version changed

When the update has includes, the result is the number of rows affected in the main entity.

docs.title: Update all the properties of a record
docs.text:
Without a filter, update filters by the primary key, whose value is taken from the data passed.

Lambda:

Orders.update()

SQL Result:

UPDATE Orders o SET
    CustomerID = ?,
    EmployeeID = ?,
    OrderDate = ?,
    RequiredDate = ?,
    ShippedDate = ?,
    ShipVia = ?,
    Freight = ?,
    ShipName = ?,
    ShipAddress = ?,
    ShipCity = ?,
    ShipRegion = ?,
    ShipPostalCode = ?,
    ShipCountry = ?
WHERE o.OrderID = ?

docs.title: Update one property in all the records
docs.text:
To update all the records of an entity, use updateAll instead of update. This prevents updating all the records by mistake.

Lambda:

Orders.updateAll({ postalCode: postalCode })

SQL Result:

UPDATE Orders o SET ShipPostalCode = ?

docs.title: Update one property with a filter
docs.text:
Updates the name of the order whose id is entity.id.

Lambda:

Orders.update({ name: entity.name }).filter(p => p.id === entity.id)

SQL Result:

UPDATE Orders o SET ShipName = ? WHERE o.OrderID = ?

docs.title: Update with a related entity
docs.text:
Updates the name of an order and, for each detail sent, all the properties of the detail. Each detail is filtered by its primary key.

Lambda:

Orders.update({ name: entity.name })
    .include(p => p.details.update(p => p))
    .filter(p => p.id === entity.id)

SQL Result:

-- the order
UPDATE Orders o SET ShipName = ?
WHERE o.OrderID = ?

-- each detail sent
UPDATE `Order Details` o1 SET UnitPrice = ?,Quantity = ?,Discount = ?
WHERE (o1.OrderID = ? AND o1.ProductID = ?)

docs.title: Update fields of the related entity
docs.text:
Updates the name of an order and only the unit price of each detail sent. In the update of the relation, unitPrice is the value sent for each detail.

Lambda:

Orders.update({ name: entity.name })
    .include(p => p.details.update(p => ({ unitPrice: unitPrice })))
    .filter(p => p.id === entity.id)

SQL Result:

-- the order
UPDATE Orders o SET ShipName = ?
WHERE o.OrderID = ?

-- each detail sent
UPDATE `Order Details` o1 SET UnitPrice = ?
WHERE (o1.OrderID = ? AND o1.ProductID = ?)

Note

Inside the update of a relation, p.unitPrice refers to the current value of the column, not to the value sent: p.details.update(p => ({ unitPrice: p.unitPrice })) generates SET UnitPrice = o1.UnitPrice, which leaves the column as it is.

docs.title: Update an entity and several related entities
docs.text:
Updates a customer, its orders and the details of each order.

Lambda:

Customers.update().include(p => p.orders.include(p => p.details))

SQL Result:

-- the customer
UPDATE Customers c SET CustomerID = ?,CompanyName = ?,ContactName = ?,ContactTitle = ?,Address = ?,City = ?,Region = ?,PostalCode = ?,Country = ?
WHERE c.CustomerID = ?

-- each order of the customer
UPDATE Orders o SET CustomerID = ?,EmployeeID = ?,OrderDate = ?,RequiredDate = ?,ShippedDate = ?,ShipVia = ?,Freight = ?,ShipName = ?,ShipAddress = ?,ShipCity = ?,ShipRegion = ?,ShipPostalCode = ?,ShipCountry = ?
WHERE o.OrderID = ?

-- details is a composite relation included as it is: each detail sent is inserted or updated (upsert),
-- and the details of the order that were not sent are deleted (see "Update an aggregate" below)
INSERT INTO `Order Details`(OrderID,ProductID,UnitPrice,Quantity,Discount) VALUES(?,?,?,?,?)
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE UnitPrice = VALUES(UnitPrice),Quantity = VALUES(Quantity),Discount = VALUES(Discount)

docs.title: Update an aggregate (composite relation)
docs.text:
When the included relation is composite (composite: true) and is included as it is (include(p => p.lines)), the update saves the whole aggregate:

  • children sent that already exist are updated,
  • children sent that do not exist are inserted (with the parent's key),
  • children of the parent that were not sent are deleted,
  • if the relation is absent from the data, the children are untouched.

The child entity needs a primary key. In this example, Orders has a composite relation lines:

domain:
  entities:
    - name: Orders
      primaryKey: [id]
      properties:
        - { name: id, length: 36, required: true }
        - { name: status, length: 20, required: true }
      relations:
        - { name: lines, type: manyToOne, composite: true, from: id, entity: OrderLines, to: orderId }
    - name: OrderLines
      primaryKey: [orderId, line]
      properties:
        - { name: orderId, length: 36, required: true }
        - { name: line, type: integer, required: true }
        - { name: product, length: 40, required: true }
        - { name: quantity, type: integer }

Lambda:

const [order] = await orm.execute('Orders.filter(p => p.id == id).include(p => p.lines)', { id: orderId })
const kept = { ...order.lines.find(p => p.line === 1), quantity: 7 } // updated
const added = { orderId, line: 3, product: 'c', quantity: 3 }        // inserted
// line 2 is not sent: deleted
await orm.execute('Orders.update().include(p => p.lines)', { ...order, status: 'sent', lines: [kept, added] })

SQL Result (PostgreSQL):

UPDATE orders o SET status = $1 WHERE o.id = $2
-- one per child sent
INSERT INTO order_lines(order_id,line,product,quantity) VALUES($1,$2,$3,$4)
ON CONFLICT (order_id,line) DO UPDATE SET product = EXCLUDED.product, quantity = EXCLUDED.quantity
-- the children not sent
DELETE FROM order_lines WHERE order_id = $1 AND NOT ((order_id = $2 AND line = $3) OR (order_id = $4 AND line = $5))

It is supported on PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server and Oracle (these two from @lambdaorm/lib 3.5.0), which save the children with upsert. On MongoDB the composite children are embedded in the parent's document, so they are replaced there.

To only update the children sent (without inserting or deleting), include the relation with an explicit update: Orders.update().include(p => p.lines.update(l => ({ quantity: quantity }))). Inside it, quantity is the value sent for each child (see Update fields of the related entity).

docs.title: Code example
docs.text:
Updates a customer with its orders and their details, and prints the number of customers updated.

import { Customers } from './domain/model' // model generated by `lambdaorm build`

(async () => {
    try {
        await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml')
        // customer with its orders and their details
        const customer = {
            id: 'ALFKI',
            name: 'Alfreds Futterkiste',
            contact: 'Maria Anders',
            phone: 'Sales Representative',
            address: 'Obere Str. 57',
            city: 'Berlin',
            region: null,
            postalCode: '12209',
            country: 'Germany',
            orders: [
                {
                    id: 1,
                    customerId: 'ALFKI',
                    employeeId: 6,
                    orderDate: '1997-08-24T22:00:00.000Z',
                    requiredDate: '1997-09-21T22:00:00.000Z',
                    shippedDate: '1997-09-01T22:00:00.000Z',
                    shipViaId: 1,
                    freight: '29.4600',
                    name: 'Alfreds Futterkiste',
                    address: 'Obere Str. 57',
                    city: 'Berlin',
                    region: null,
                    postalCode: '12209',
                    country: 'Germany',
                    details: [
                        {
                            orderId: 1,
                            productId: 28,
                            unitPrice: '45.6000',
                            quantity: '15.0000',
                            discount: '0.0000'
                        },
                        {
                            orderId: 1,
                            productId: 39,

                        },
                        {
                            orderId: 1,

                            discount: '0.0000'
                        }
                    ]
                },
                {
                    id: 2,

                    employeeId: 4,

})()

docs.title: Bitwise Operators
docs.text:
Bitwise operators work on the binary representation of integer values.

About the examples

The examples run against the Countries entity of the countries sample schema. Each one shows the query, the result it returned on the test database and the SQL sentence that λORM generated for MySQL. Other engines receive their own translation; to see the sentence generated for your data source, use orm.plan.

Results on MySQL

MySQL evaluates bitwise operations as unsigned 64-bit integers. The longitude of Brazil is -55, so several of the results below are very large numbers.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Operator Description ~ Bitwise NOT & Bitwise AND | Bitwise OR ^ Bitwise XOR (exclusive OR); it is not exponentiation, use ** for that << Left shift >> Right shift

docs.title: Bitwise NOT (~)
docs.text:
Inverts all the bits of a. Operands and result are numbers.

Syntax: ~a

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3=="BRA").first(p=> {result: ~ p.longitude })

Result: [{"result":54}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT ~ c.longitude AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'
ORDER BY result asc
LIMIT 0,1

docs.title: Bitwise AND (&)
docs.text:
Each bit of the result is 1 when the corresponding bits of a and b are both 1. Operands and result are numbers.

Syntax: a & b

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3=="BRA").first(p=> {result: p.longitude & 1 })

Result: [{"result":1}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT c.longitude & 1 AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'
ORDER BY result asc
LIMIT 0,1

docs.title: Bitwise OR (|)
docs.text:
Each bit of the result is 1 when the corresponding bit of a or of b is 1. Operands and result are numbers.

Syntax: a | b

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3=="BRA").first(p=> {result: p.longitude | 1 })

Result: [{"result":18446744073709552000}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT c.longitude | 1 AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'
ORDER BY result asc
LIMIT 0,1

docs.title: Bitwise XOR (^)
docs.text:
Each bit of the result is 1 when the corresponding bits of a and b are different. Operands and result are numbers.

Syntax: a ^ b

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3=="BRA").first(p=> {result: p.longitude ^ 1 })

Result: [{"result":18446744073709552000}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT c.longitude ^ 1 AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'
ORDER BY result asc
LIMIT 0,1

docs.title: Left shift (<<)
docs.text:
Shifts the bits of a to the left by b positions. Operands and result are numbers.

Syntax: a << b

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3=="BRA").first(p=> {result: p.longitude << 1 })

Result: [{"result":18446744073709552000}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT c.longitude << 1 AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'
ORDER BY result asc
LIMIT 0,1

docs.title: Right shift (>>)
docs.text:
Shifts the bits of a to the right by b positions. Operands and result are numbers.

Syntax: a >> b

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3=="BRA").first(p=> {result: p.longitude >> 1 })

Result: [{"result":9223372036854776000}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT c.longitude >> 1 AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'
ORDER BY result asc
LIMIT 0,1

docs.title: Database support
docs.text:
Engine differences

  • Oracle: &, | and ^ are translated to BITAND, BITOR and BITXOR.
  • PostgreSQL: ^ is translated to the # operator (XOR).
  • MongoDB: bitwise operators cannot currently be translated to MongoDB queries.

docs.title: Comparison Operators and Functions
docs.text:
Comparison operators and functions compare two or more values and return a boolean. They are mostly used in the predicate of filter (the WHERE clause of the generated SQL), but they can be used in any expression of a query.

About the examples

The examples run against the Countries entity of the countries sample schema. Each one shows the query, the result it returned on the test database and the SQL sentence that λORM generated for MySQL. Other engines receive their own translation; to see the sentence generated for your data source, use orm.plan.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Operator / function Description ==, === Equal to !=, !==, <> Not equal to > Greater than < Less than >= Greater than or equal to <= Less than or equal to between Checks whether a value is within a range in Checks whether a value is in a list of values includes Checks whether a list contains a value

docs.title: Equal (==, ===)
docs.text:
Returns true when both operands are equal. == and === are equivalent: both are translated to = in SQL.

Syntax:

  • a == b
  • a === b
Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> p.name)

Result: [{"name":"Brazil"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT c.name AS name
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 === "BRA").map(p=> p.name)

Result: [{"name":"Brazil"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT c.name AS name
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: Not equal (!=, !==, <>)
docs.text:
Returns true when the operands are different. The three forms are equivalent and are translated to <> in SQL.

Syntax:

  • a != b
  • a !== b
  • a <> b

See the Logical page for an example that uses !=.

docs.title: Greater than, less than (>, <, >=, <=)
docs.text:
Compare two values of the same type (numbers, strings or dates).

  • a > b: a is greater than b.
  • a < b: a is less than b.
  • a >= b: a is greater than or equal to b.
  • a <= b: a is less than or equal to b.

Name of the first country (ordered by name) whose latitude is between -11 and -9 (exclusive) and whose longitude is -55:

Countries.filter(p=> p.latitude < -9 && p.latitude > -11 && p.longitude == -55 ).first(p=> p.name)

Result: [{"name":"Brazil"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT c.name AS name
FROM Countries c
WHERE (c.latitude < -9 AND (c.latitude > -11 AND c.longitude = -55))
ORDER BY c.name asc
LIMIT 0,1

docs.title: between
docs.text:
Returns true when value is within the range from to to. In SQL it is translated to value BETWEEN from AND to, which includes both limits.

Signature: between(value: T, from: T, to: T): boolean

Countries.filter(p=> between(p.latitude,-11,-9) && p.longitude == -55 ).first(p=> p.name)

Result: [{"name":"Brazil"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT c.name AS name
FROM Countries c
WHERE (c.latitude BETWEEN -11 AND -9 AND c.longitude = -55)
ORDER BY c.name asc
LIMIT 0,1

docs.title: in
docs.text:
Returns true when value is equal to one of the values of list. It replaces several conditions joined with ||, and is translated to value IN (...) in SQL.

Signature: in(value: T, list: T[]): boolean

Countries.filter(p=> in(p.iso3,["BRA","ARG"])).map(p=> p.name)

Result: [{"name":"Argentina"},{"name":"Brazil"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT c.name AS name
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 IN ('BRA', 'ARG')

docs.title: includes
docs.text:
Returns true when list contains value. It is the same check as in, with the arguments in the opposite order: the list comes first. contains is an alias of includes.

Signature: includes(list: T[], value: T): boolean

For example, includes(["BRA","ARG"], p.iso3) generates the same WHERE c.iso3 IN ('BRA', 'ARG') condition as the in example above on MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQLite.

docs.title: Database support
docs.text:
Engine differences

  • MongoDB: between is translated to {"$gte": from, "$lt": to}, so the upper limit is excluded, unlike SQL BETWEEN. includes cannot currently be translated to a MongoDB query; use in instead.
  • SQL Server: includes is translated to a LIKE (text search) instead of IN; use in to check a value against a list.

docs.title: Date and Time Functions
docs.text:
Date and time functions get the current date and time, convert strings to dates, extract parts of a date, add intervals to a date and calculate the difference between two dates.

About the examples

The examples run against the Countries entity of the countries sample schema. Each one shows the query, the result it returned on the test database and the SQL sentence that λORM generated for MySQL. Other engines receive their own translation; to see the sentence generated for your data source, use orm.plan.

Results depend on the engine and the time zone

Date and time values are calculated by the database. The results below were obtained on MySQL in a session that was not in UTC, so some values (for example those of date, time or hour) are shifted by the time zone. Expect different values on other engines or time zones.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Function Description now Current date and time today Current date curTime Current time dateTime Converts a string to a date and time date Converts a string to a date time Converts a string to a time dateToString Converts a date to an ISO 8601 string year Year of a date month Month of a date day Day of the month of a date weekday Day of the week of a date hour Hour of a date minute Minute of a date second Second of a date millisecond Millisecond of a date addYear Adds years to a date addMonth Adds months to a date addDay Adds days to a date addHour Adds hours to a date addMinute Adds minutes to a date addSecond Adds seconds to a date addMillisecond Adds milliseconds to a date addTime Adds a time to a date subtractTime Subtracts a time from a date dayDiff Difference between two dates in days hourDiff Difference between two dates in hours secondDiff Difference between two dates in seconds millisecondDiff Difference between two dates in milliseconds dayToDate Date for a number of days since 1970-01-01 hourToDate Date for a number of hours since 1970-01-01 secondToDate Date for a number of seconds since 1970-01-01 millisecondToDate Date for a number of milliseconds since 1970-01-01

docs.title: now
docs.text:
Returns the current date and time.

Signature: now(): dateTime

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:now()})

Result: [{"result":"2022-08-15T09:54:22.000Z"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT NOW() AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: today
docs.text:
Returns the current date.

Signature: today(): date

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:today()})

Result: [{"result":"2022-08-14T22:00:00.000Z"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT CURDATE() AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: curTime
docs.text:
Returns the current time.

Signature: curTime(): time

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:curTime()})

Result: [{"result":"11:54:22"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT CURTIME() AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: dateTime
docs.text:
Converts value to a date and time.

Signature: dateTime(value: string): dateTime

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:dateTime("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z")})

Result: [{"result":"2021-09-06T12:39:11.000Z"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT CONVERT('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z', DATETIME) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: date
docs.text:
Converts value to a date (without the time).

Signature: date(value: string): date

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:date("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z")})

Result: [{"result":"2021-09-05T22:00:00.000Z"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT CONVERT('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z', DATE) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: time
docs.text:
Converts value to a time (without the date).

Signature: time(value: string): time

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:time("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z")})

Result: [{"result":"00:20:21"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT CONVERT('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z', TIME) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: dateToString
docs.text:
Converts date to a string in ISO 8601 format.

Signature: dateToString(date: dateTime): string

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:dateToString(dateTime("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z"))})

Result: [{"result":"2021-09-06T14:39:11Z"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT DATE_FORMAT(CONVERT('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z', DATETIME), '%Y-%m-%dT%TZ') AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: Date parts
docs.text: These functions return a part of a date as an integer.

docs.title: year
docs.text:
Returns the year of value.

Signature: year(value: dateTime): integer

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:year("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z")})

Result: [{"result":2021}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM '2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z') AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: month
docs.text:
Returns the month of value (1 to 12).

Signature: month(value: dateTime): integer

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:month("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z")})

Result: [{"result":9}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT EXTRACT(MONTH FROM '2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z') AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: day
docs.text:
Returns the day of the month of value.

Signature: day(value: dateTime): integer

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:day("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z")})

Result: [{"result":6}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT DAYOFMONTH('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z') AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: weekday
docs.text:
Returns the day of the week of value. The numbering depends on the engine: on MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite (DAYOFWEEK) 1 is Sunday and 7 is Saturday, so the example (a Monday) returns 2; on PostgreSQL (extract(dow ...)) 0 is Sunday.

Signature: weekday(value: dateTime): integer

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:weekday("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z")})

Result: [{"result":2}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT DAYOFWEEK('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z') AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: hour
docs.text:
Returns the hour of value.

Signature: hour(value: dateTime): integer

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:hour("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z")})

Result: [{"result":0}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT EXTRACT(HOUR FROM '2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z') AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: minute
docs.text:
Returns the minute of value.

Signature: minute(value: dateTime): integer

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:minute("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z")})

Result: [{"result":20}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT EXTRACT(MINUTE FROM '2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z') AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: second
docs.text:
Returns the second of value.

Signature: second(value: dateTime): integer

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:second("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z")})

Result: [{"result":21}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT EXTRACT(SECOND FROM '2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z') AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: millisecond
docs.text:
Returns the millisecond of value.

Signature: millisecond(value: dateTime): integer

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:millisecond("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z")})

Result: [{"result":0}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT ROUND(EXTRACT(MICROSECOND FROM '2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z')/1000,0) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: Adding intervals
docs.text: These functions add value units to date and return the new date. Use a negative value to subtract.

docs.title: addYear
docs.text:
Adds value years to date.

Signature: addYear(date: dateTime, value: number): dateTime

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:addYear("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z",2)})

Result: [{"result":"2023-09-06 14:39:11.444000"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT DATE_ADD('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z', INTERVAL 2 YEAR) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: addMonth
docs.text:
Adds value months to date.

Signature: addMonth(date: dateTime, value: number): dateTime

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:addMonth("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z",2)})

Result: [{"result":"2021-11-06 14:39:11.444000"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT DATE_ADD('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z', INTERVAL 2 MONTH) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: addDay
docs.text:
Adds value days to date.

Signature: addDay(date: dateTime, value: number): dateTime

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:addDay("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z",2)})

Result: [{"result":"2021-09-08 14:39:11.444000"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT DATE_ADD('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z', INTERVAL 2 DAY) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: addHour
docs.text:
Adds value hours to date.

Signature: addHour(date: dateTime, value: number): dateTime

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:addHour("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z",2)})

Result: [{"result":"2021-09-06 16:39:11.444000"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT '2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z' + interval '2' HOUR AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: addMinute
docs.text:
Adds value minutes to date.

Signature: addMinute(date: dateTime, value: number): dateTime

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:addMinute("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z",2)})

Result: [{"result":"2021-09-06 14:41:11.444000"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT '2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z' + interval '2' MINUTE AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: addSecond
docs.text:
Adds value seconds to date.

Signature: addSecond(date: dateTime, value: number): dateTime

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:addSecond("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z",2)})

Result: [{"result":"2021-09-06 14:39:13.444000"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT '2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z' + interval '2' SECOND AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: addMillisecond
docs.text:
Adds value milliseconds to date.

Signature: addMillisecond(date: dateTime, value: number): dateTime

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:addMillisecond("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z",2)})

Result: [{"result":"2021-09-06 14:39:11.446000"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT DATE_ADD('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z', INTERVAL (2 * 1000) MICROSECOND) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: addTime
docs.text:
Adds time to date.

Signature: addTime(date: dateTime, time: time): dateTime

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:addTime("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z","08:22:12")})

Result: [{"result":"08:42:33"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT ADDTIME('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z','08:22:12') AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: subtractTime
docs.text:
Subtracts time from date.

Signature: subtractTime(date: dateTime, time: time): dateTime

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:subtractTime("2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z","08:22:12")})

Result: [{"result":"-08:01:51"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT SUBTIME('2021-09-06T14:39:11.444Z','08:22:12') AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: Differences between dates
docs.text: These functions return date1 - date2 in the given unit, as an integer.

docs.title: dayDiff
docs.text:
Returns the difference between date1 and date2 in days.

Signature: dayDiff(date1: dateTime, date2: dateTime): integer

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:dayDiff("2021-09-06T14:39:11","2021-09-02T12:30:10")})

Result: [{"result":4}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT DATEDIFF('2021-09-06T14:39:11','2021-09-02T12:30:10') AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: hourDiff
docs.text:
Returns the difference between date1 and date2 in hours.

Signature: hourDiff(date1: dateTime, date2: dateTime): integer

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:hourDiff("2021-09-06T14:39:11","2021-09-02T12:30:10")})

Result: [{"result":98}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT TIMESTAMPDIFF(HOUR, '2021-09-02T12:30:10','2021-09-06T14:39:11') AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: secondDiff
docs.text:
Returns the difference between date1 and date2 in seconds.

Signature: secondDiff(date1: dateTime, date2: dateTime): integer

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:secondDiff("2021-09-06T14:39:11","2021-09-02T12:30:10")})

Result: [{"result":353341}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, '2021-09-02T12:30:10','2021-09-06T14:39:11') AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: millisecondDiff
docs.text:
Returns the difference between date1 and date2 in milliseconds.

Signature: millisecondDiff(date1: dateTime, date2: dateTime): integer

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:millisecondDiff("2021-09-06T14:39:11","2021-09-02T12:30:10")})

Result: [{"result":353341000}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT ROUND(TIMESTAMPDIFF(MICROSECOND, '2021-09-02T12:30:10','2021-09-06T14:39:11')/1000,0) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: Numbers to dates
docs.text: These functions convert a number of time units elapsed since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z (the Unix epoch) to a date.

docs.title: dayToDate
docs.text:
Returns the date that is value days after the Unix epoch.

Signature: dayToDate(value: number): dateTime

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:dayToDate(2000)})

Result: [{"result":"1975-06-24T00:00:00Z"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT DATE_FORMAT(FROM_UNIXTIME(2000*24*3600), '%Y-%m-%dT%TZ') AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: hourToDate
docs.text:
Returns the date that is value hours after the Unix epoch.

Signature: hourToDate(value: number): dateTime

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:hourToDate(2000)})

Result: [{"result":"1970-03-25T08:00:00Z"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT DATE_FORMAT(FROM_UNIXTIME(2000*3600), '%Y-%m-%dT%TZ') AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: secondToDate
docs.text:
Returns the date that is value seconds after the Unix epoch.

Signature: secondToDate(value: number): dateTime

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:secondToDate(2000)})

Result: [{"result":"1970-01-01T00:33:20Z"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT DATE_FORMAT(FROM_UNIXTIME(2000), '%Y-%m-%dT%TZ') AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: millisecondToDate
docs.text:
Returns the date that is value milliseconds after the Unix epoch.

Signature: millisecondToDate(value: number): dateTime

Countries.filter(p=> p.iso3 == "BRA").map(p=> {result:millisecondToDate(2000)})

Result: [{"result":"1970-01-01T00:00:02Z"}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT DATE_FORMAT(FROM_UNIXTIME(2000/1000), '%Y-%m-%dT%TZ') AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.iso3 = 'BRA'

docs.title: Database support
docs.text:
MongoDB

In the current version, only now, today, date, year, month, day and weekday can be translated to MongoDB queries. The other date and time functions on this page are not available on MongoDB.

docs.title: Aggregate Functions
docs.text:
Aggregate (group) functions calculate a single value from a set of rows. When a query's map mixes aggregate functions with other fields, λORM groups the rows by those other fields (GROUP BY in SQL). See Grouping for more examples, including having.

About the examples

The examples run against the Countries entity of the countries sample schema. Each one shows the query, the result it returned on the test database and the SQL sentence that λORM generated for MySQL. Other engines receive their own translation; to see the sentence generated for your data source, use orm.plan.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Function Description avg Average of the values count Number of rows first First value of the set last Last value of the set max Maximum value min Minimum value sum Sum of the values

docs.title: count
docs.text:
Returns the number of rows in the set. count(1) counts all the rows.

Signature: count(value: any): integer

Number of countries in the Americas region:

Countries.filter(p=> p.region == "Americas").map(p=> {result:count(1)})

Result: [{"result":57}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT COUNT(1) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE c.region = 'Americas'

Number of countries in each region:

Countries.map(p=> {region:p.region,countries:count(1)})

Result:

[{"region":"","countries":2}
,{"region":"Africa","countries":60}
,{"region":"Americas","countries":57}
,{"region":"Asia","countries":50}
,{"region":"Europe","countries":53}
,{"region":"Oceania","countries":27}
,{"region":"Polar","countries":1}
]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT c.region AS region, COUNT(1) AS countries
FROM Countries c
GROUP BY c.region

docs.title: max
docs.text:
Returns the maximum value of the set.

Signature: max(value: T): T

Maximum latitude of the countries of each region:

Countries.map(p=> {region:p.region,max:max(p.latitude)})

Result:

[{"region":"","max":-53.1}
,{"region":"Africa","max":34}
,{"region":"Americas","max":72}
,{"region":"Asia","max":48}
,{"region":"Europe","max":78}
,{"region":"Oceania","max":15.2}
,{"region":"Polar","max":-74.65}
]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT c.region AS region, MAX(c.latitude) AS max
FROM Countries c
GROUP BY c.region

docs.title: min
docs.text:
Returns the minimum value of the set.

Signature: min(value: T): T

Minimum latitude of the countries of each region:

Countries.map(p=> {region:p.region,min:min(p.latitude)})

Result:

[{"region":"","min":-54.4333}
,{"region":"Africa","min":-49.25}
,{"region":"Americas","min":-54.5}
,{"region":"Asia","min":-8.8333}
,{"region":"Europe","min":35}
,{"region":"Oceania","min":-41}
,{"region":"Polar","min":-74.65}
]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT c.region AS region, MIN(c.latitude) AS min
FROM Countries c
GROUP BY c.region

docs.title: avg
docs.text:
Returns the average of the values of the set.

Signature: avg(value: number): number

Average latitude of the countries of each region:

Countries.map(p=> {region:p.region,avg:avg(p.latitude)})

Result:

[{"region":"","avg":-53.76665}
,{"region":"Africa","avg":1.283335}
,{"region":"Americas","avg":10.42610526}
,{"region":"Asia","avg":25.822002}
,{"region":"Europe","avg":49.35021321}
,{"region":"Oceania","avg":-10.93023704}
,{"region":"Polar","avg":-74.65}
]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT c.region AS region, AVG(c.latitude) AS avg
FROM Countries c
GROUP BY c.region

docs.title: sum
docs.text:
Returns the sum of the values of the set. It is translated to SUM(...) in SQL.

Signature: sum(value: number): number

docs.title: first
docs.text:
Returns the first value of the set.

Signature: first(value: T): T

docs.title: last
docs.text:
Returns the last value of the set.

Signature: last(value: T): T

first and last on SQL databases

On SQL databases, first and last used as aggregates are translated to FIRST(...) and LAST(...); check that your database engine supports these aggregate functions. On MongoDB they are translated to $first and $last.

Do not confuse them with the first and last query methods (for example Countries.first(p=> p.name)), which return the first or last row of a query; see Select.

docs.title: Logical Operators
docs.text:
Logical operators combine or negate boolean expressions, for example to join several conditions in the predicate of filter.

About the examples

The examples run against the Countries entity of the countries sample schema. Each one shows the query, the result it returned on the test database and the SQL sentence that λORM generated for MySQL. Other engines receive their own translation; to see the sentence generated for your data source, use orm.plan.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Operator Description SQL ! Logical NOT NOT && Logical AND AND || Logical OR OR

docs.title: NOT (!)
docs.text:
Negates a boolean expression: returns true when value is false, and false when it is true.

Syntax: !value

For example, Countries.filter(p=> !(p.iso3 == "BRA")) generates the condition WHERE NOT c.iso3 = 'BRA'.

docs.title: AND (&&)
docs.text:
Returns true when both operands are true.

Syntax: a && b

Number of countries in South America whose longitude is less than -30:

Countries.filter(p=> p.subregion == "South America" &&  p.longitude < -30 ).map(p=> {result:count(1)})

Result: [{"result":15}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT COUNT(1) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE (c.subregion = 'South America' AND c.longitude < -30)

docs.title: OR (||)
docs.text:
Returns true when at least one of the operands is true.

Syntax: a || b

Number of countries in South America or Central America:

Countries.filter(p=> p.subregion == "South America" || p.subregion == "Central America" ).map(p=> {result:count(1)})

Result: [{"result":23}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT COUNT(1) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE (c.subregion = 'South America' OR c.subregion = 'Central America')

docs.title: Combining conditions
docs.text:
Operators can be combined with the comparison operators described in Comparison. Number of countries in the Americas region that are not in Northern America:

Countries.filter(p=> p.region == "Americas" &&  p.subregion != "Northern America" ).map(p=> {result:count(1)})

Result: [{"result":51}]

Generated SQL (MySQL):

SELECT COUNT(1) AS result
FROM Countries c
WHERE (c.region = 'Americas' AND c.subregion <> 'Northern America')

docs.title: Nullable Functions
docs.text:
Nullable functions check whether a value is null, or replace null values with another value.

About the examples
