      fields: ["city"]
    properties:
    - name: address
    - name: city
    - name: region
    - name: postalCode
      length: 20
    - name: country
  - name: Categories
    primaryKey: ["id"]
    uniqueKey: ["name"]
    properties:
    - name: id
      type: integer
      required: true
      autoIncrement: true
    - name: name
      required: true
  - name: Customers
    extends: Address
    primaryKey: ["id"]
    indexes:
    - name: name
      fields: ["name"]
    properties:
    - name: id
      length: 5
      required: true
    - name: name
      required: true
  - name: Products
    primaryKey: ["id"]
    uniqueKey: ["name", "supplierId"]
    properties:
    - name: id
      type: integer
      required: true
      autoIncrement: true
    - name: name
      required: true
    - name: categoryId
      type: integer
    - name: quantity
    - name: price
      type: decimal
      default: 0
    relations:
    - name: category
      from: categoryId
      entity: Categories
      to: id
      target: products
  - name: Orders
    primaryKey: ["id"]
    indexes:
    - name: orderDate
      fields: ["orderDate"]
    properties:

docs.title: Extend
docs.text:
This page shows how to reuse definitions with the extends key.

With extends, an element of the schema inherits the definition of another one. Enums, entities, mappings and entity mappings can be extended.

docs.title: Extend Entity
docs.text:
In this schema, the entities Countries and States extend the abstract entity Positions, so both get the properties latitude and longitude. An entity does not need to be abstract to be extended; an abstract entity is only a base and has no table.

domain:
  entities:
    - name: Positions
      abstract: true
      properties:
        - name: latitude
          length: 16
        - name: longitude
          length: 16
    - name: Countries
      extends: Positions
      primaryKey: ["iso3"]
      uniqueKey: ["name"]
      properties:
        - name: name
          required: true
        - name: iso3
          length: 3
          required: true
      relations:
        - name: states
          type: manyToOne
          composite: true
          from: iso3
          entity: States
          to: countryCode
    - name: States
      extends: Positions
      primaryKey: ["id"]
      uniqueKey: ["countryCode", "name"]
      properties:
        - name: id
          type: integer
          required: true
        - name: name
          required: true
        - name: countryCode
          required: true
          length: 3
      relations:
        - name: country
          from: countryCode
          entity: Countries
          to: iso3
infrastructure:          
  sources:
    - name: source1
      dialect: MySQL
      connection:
        host: localhost
        port: 3306
        user: test
        password: test
        database: test

docs.title: Extend mappings
docs.text: Mappings and entity mappings are extended in the same way. See Abstract and extends in Entity Mapping, and the mapping mongoDb, which extends the mapping default, in the Listener example.

docs.title: Listener on Schema
docs.text:
This page explains listeners: expressions that λORM runs before or after a query, or when it fails. They are defined in application.listeners (see Listener).

  • on: the categories of query that trigger the listener: select, insert, upsert, update and delete. A bulk insert belongs to the insert category, and a merge to the upsert category.
  • condition: an expression that decides whether the listener runs.
  • before, after and error: the expressions to run before the query, after it, or when it fails.
  • transactional: whether the listener runs inside the query's transaction (default true).

docs.title: How listeners run
docs.text:
• before, after and error run one after the other and are awaited: orm.execute returns when they have finished. An error in before prevents the sentence; an error in after fails it (the error listeners run first).
  • They run in the sentence's transaction: the orm.execute calls of a listener use the same connections, and a rollback undoes what they wrote. A sentence with listeners that runs on its own opens a transaction for the sentence and its listeners, so both are all or nothing.
  • A listener's orm.execute can name another stage ({ stage: "insights" }): it joins the same transaction (since @lambdaorm/lib 3.3.0).
  • transactional: false runs a listener outside the transaction: what it writes is kept even if the transaction rolls back (for example, an audit log).

In this example, touchInstallation updates the installation of each inserted file in the same transaction, and audit writes an audit log that is kept even if the transaction rolls back:

application:
  listeners:
    - name: touchInstallation
      on: [insert]
      condition: entity == "InstallationFiles"
      after: >-
        orm.execute("Installations.update(p => ({ lastEventAt: at })).filter(p => p.id == id)",
          { id: data.installationId, at: data.uploadedAt })
    - name: audit
      on: [insert, update, delete]
      transactional: false
      after: orm.execute("AuditLogs.insert()", { entity: entity, action: action })

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
The arguments available in condition, before, after and error:

Parameter Description query The query expression that was executed data The data that was sent when the expression was executed options The options that were sent when the expression was executed result It is only available in the after event and contains the result of the expression execution action The action that was executed (select, insert, bulkInsert, update, upsert, merge, bulkMerge, delete, bulkDelete) type The type of sentence that was executed (dql, dml) category The category of the sentence that was executed (select, insert, update, delete, upsert) sentence The sentence that was executed dialect The dialect of the source where the sentence was executed source The source where the sentence was executed entity The entity that was affected by the sentence error It is only available in the error event and contains the error that occurred

docs.title: Listener Example
docs.text:
This example declares a listener that copies the data to the insights stage (CQRS pattern). When records are inserted, updated or deleted on the default or cqrs stage, the listener runs. Its after expression executes the same query, with the same data, on the insights stage, in the same transaction as the original query: if the write in insights fails, the original one is rolled back too.

Part of the schema where the listener is defined:

...
application:
  listeners:
    - name: syncInsights
      on: [insert, update, delete]
      condition: options.stage.in("default","cqrs")
      after: orm.execute(query,data,{stage:"insights"})

Complete schema:

docs.title: Multiple Stages
docs.text:
This page shows a schema with two stages: the same model stored in two different databases.

A stage is a usage scenario. Several stages can be defined for different reasons, for example:

  • To run the same business model on Oracle and on SQL Server and compare their performance.
  • To use one stage as the origin and another as the destination of a data migration.
  • To use one stage for reads and another for writes.
  • To use one stage for the development environment and another for the QA environment.

docs.title: Schema Example
docs.text:
In this schema, stage1 uses a MySQL database with the default names (mapping1 is empty), and stage2 uses a PostgreSQL database whose tables and columns have other names (mapping2). The same query gives the same result on both stages.

domain:
  entities:
    - name: Countries
      primaryKey: ["iso3"]
      uniqueKey: ["name"]
      properties:
        - name: name
          required: true
        - name: iso3
          length: 3
          required: true
      relations:
        - name: states
          type: manyToOne
          composite: true
          from: iso3
          entity: States
          to: countryCode
    - name: States
      primaryKey: ["id"]
      uniqueKey: ["countryCode", "name"]
      properties:
        - name: id
          type: integer
          required: true
        - name: name
          required: true
        - name: countryCode
          required: true
          length: 3
      relations:
        - name: country
          from: countryCode
          entity: Countries
          to: iso3
infrastructure:
  mappings:
    - name: mapping1
    - name: mapping2
      entities:
        - name: Countries
          mapping: TBL_COUNTRIES
          properties:
            - name: iso3
              mapping: ISO3
            - name: name
              mapping: NAME
        - name: States
          mapping: TBL_STATES
          properties:
            - name: id
              mapping: ID
            - name: name
              mapping: NAME
            - name: countryCode
              mapping: COUNTRY_CODE
  sources:
    - name: source1
      dialect: MySQL
      mapping: mapping1
      connection: $CNN_MYSQL
    - name: source2
      dialect: PostgreSQL
      mapping: mapping2
      connection: $CNN_POSTGRES
  stages:
    - name: stage1
      sources:
        - name: source1
    - name: stage2
      sources:
        - name: source2

Environment variables:

CNN_MYSQL={"host":"localhost","port":3306,"user":"test","password":"test","database":"test"}
CNN_POSTGRES={"host":"0.0.0.0","port":5433,"user":"test","password":"test","database":"test"}

docs.title: Stage with Multiple Sources
docs.text:
This page shows a stage whose entities are stored in different databases, first with the same mapping and then with a different mapping for each source.

  • When the entities are in different databases, the stage says which source each entity uses.
  • This is done with the condition of each source rule: an expression evaluated for each entity; when it is true, that source is used.
  • The conditions are evaluated in the order of the stage, so when an entity meets the conditions of two sources, the first one is used. A source without condition takes the entities that no previous source took.

docs.title: Multiple sources sharing the mapping
docs.text:
In this schema, States is stored in a PostgreSQL database (dataSource2) and every other entity in a MySQL database (dataSource1). Both sources use the same mapping (the default one, since none is defined), so the tables and columns have the same names as the entities and properties.

          composite: true
          from: iso3
          entity: States
          to: countryCode
    - name: States
      primaryKey: ["id"]
      uniqueKey: ["countryCode", "name"]
      properties:
        - name: id
          type: integer
          required: true
        - name: name
          required: true
        - name: countryCode
          required: true
          length: 3
      relations:
        - name: country
          from: countryCode
          entity: Countries
          to: iso3
infrastructure:          
  sources:
    - name: dataSource1
      dialect: MySQL
      connection:
        host: localhost
        port: 3306
        user: test
        password: test
        database: test
    - name: dataSource2
      dialect: PostgreSQL
      connection:
        host: localhost
        port: 5432
        user: test
        password: test
        database: test

    - name: stage1
      sources:
        - name: dataSource2
          condition: entity == "States"
        - name: dataSource1

docs.text:
In this schema, dataSource1 is a MySQL database that holds the Countries table, and dataSource2 is a PostgreSQL database that holds the States table.

For Countries, the names of the table and its columns are the same as the names of the entity and its properties, so its mapping (mapping1) is empty. For States, the names of the table and its columns are different, so mapping2 defines them.

docs.title: Fetch
docs.text: This page explains fetch, which shows the differences between the sources (databases) of a stage and the schema without applying any change: what it compares, the CLI command lambdaorm fetch and the orm.stage.fetch() method.

docs.title: What fetch compares
docs.text:
Fetch reads the databases of the stage and compares them with the model (drift). The result has one entry per mapping, with the entities that differ:

  • tables missing in the database or missing in the model,
  • columns missing on one side,
  • columns with another type, length or nullability,
  • a different primary key.

Each entity has its differences, in readable text. When the databases are in step with the model, every mapping has no entities.

Relations (foreign keys) and indexes are not compared. On MongoDB, which is schemaless, fetch only checks that each collection exists.

Example of a result, after adding the property phone to Customers in the model:

- name: default
  entities:
    - name: Customers
      mapping: customers
      differences:
        - column phone missing in the database

Result when the database is in step with the model:

- name: default
  entities: []

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
lambdaorm fetch -s default -o yaml
Option Description -w, --workspace Folder of the project (default: the current folder). -s, --stage Name of the stage (default: the first stage). -e, --envfile File of environment variables to read. -o, --output Output format: json, beautiful, light or yaml.

The command exits with code 1 when there are differences (and 0 when the databases are in step), so it can be used in CI to detect drift:

lambdaorm fetch -s default || echo "the database differs from the model"

See the CLI lab.

docs.title: Node
docs.text:
orm.stage.fetch() returns the differences. To read the mappings of the databases as they are (every table and column), use orm.stage.read().

import { Orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib'
(async () => {
    const orm = new Orm()
    try {
        await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml')
        const mappings = await orm.stage.fetch({ stage: 'default' })
        const differing: any[] = mappings.flatMap(p => p.entities || [])
        for (const entity of differing) {
            console.log(entity.name, entity.differences)
        }
        // the databases' own mappings
        const database = await orm.stage.read({ stage: 'default' })
        await orm.helper.fs.write('./mappings.yaml', orm.helper.yaml.dump(database))
    } finally {
        await orm.end()
    }
})()

See the Node lab.

docs.title: Incorporate
docs.text:
This page explains incorporate, which updates the schema from a JSON data file, pushes the changes to the sources (databases) and imports the data: the CLI command lambdaorm incorporate and the orm.stage.incorporate() method.

Incorporate:

  1. Deduces the entities, properties and relations from the data and adds them to the schema file, as introspect does.
  2. Runs a push, so the databases of the stage get the new tables and columns.
  3. Imports the data into the databases.

lambdaorm incorporate -d countries.json -n countries
Option Description -d, --data JSON data file (or the data as inline JSON). Required. -n, --name Name of the root entity (default: the name of the file). -w, --workspace Folder of the project (default: the current folder). -s, --stage Name of the stage (default: the first stage). -e, --envfile File of environment variables to read.

Files generated in the orm_state folder:

│   ├── default-data.json
│   ├── default-model.json
│   └── <source>
│       └── V<yyMMddHHmmss>__push.sql

  • <stage>-data.json: the state of the import.

docs.title: Pull
docs.text: This page explains pull, which updates the schema file with the structure of the sources (databases) of a stage: what it keeps, the CLI command lambdaorm pull and the orm.stage.pull() method.

docs.title: What pull keeps
docs.text:
Pull reads the tables and columns of the databases and merges them into the schema: new tables become entities, new columns become properties, and the mappings are updated. Pull does not change the databases. By default it also removes from the schema the entities, properties and relations that are no longer in the database (orm.stage.pull({ stage, removeEntities: false, removeProperties: false, removeRelations: false }) keeps them). It can be run on an existing schema: what was written by hand is kept, for example

  • relation names chosen by hand and weak relations between sources (which have no foreign key in the database),
  • application.listeners,
  • infrastructure.stages.

Columns named with reserved words (for example order) are supported.

docs.text:
The pull command updates the schema file (lambdaORM.yaml in this example) with the structure of the databases of the stage:

Option Description -w, --workspace Folder of the project (default: the current folder). -s, --stage Name of the stage (default: the first stage). -e, --envfile File of environment variables to read.

Pull also writes, in the orm_state folder, the model of the stage and the DDL of the pulled structure, in one folder per source. The DDL is a record: it is not executed.

docs.title: Push
docs.text: This page explains push, which updates the sources (databases) of a stage with the schema: how it works, the CLI command lambdaorm push and the orm.stage.push() method.

docs.title: How push works
docs.text:
Push reads the databases of the stage (as fetch does) and generates the DDL that takes them to the model:

  • Tables that do not exist are created with their primary key, unique key, foreign keys and indexes.
  • In existing tables, missing columns are added (ALTER TABLE … ADD) and columns with another type, length or nullability are altered.
  • A column declared with previousMapping in its property mapping is renamed (ALTER TABLE … RENAME COLUMN, SqlServer sp_rename) instead of being added. See Rename a column.
  • Push never drops anything that exists only in the database (tables, columns). fetch reports it, so it can be removed by hand if needed.
  • The column types follow the property types and the dbType of the property mapping. See Property types.
  • Each entity goes to the source chosen by the stage rules; a source without condition only gets the entities no other source took.

Since the comparison is made against the databases, push works the same on any host or CI job: it does not need the orm_state folder of a previous push. The orm_state folder is still written, as a record of what was applied.

Renaming a table is not supported.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
Apply the changes:

lambdaorm push
Option Description -w, --workspace Folder of the project (default: the current folder). -s, --stage Name of the stage (default: the first stage). -e, --envfile File of environment variables to read. -o, --output Generate the DDL without applying it (see below). -f, --force When a sentence fails, continue with the next ones.

Example of the generated DDL on an empty database:

CREATE TABLE Countries (name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL ,iso3 VARCHAR(3) NOT NULL ,CONSTRAINT Countries_PK PRIMARY KEY (iso3));
ALTER TABLE Countries ADD CONSTRAINT Countries_UK UNIQUE (name);
CREATE TABLE States (id INTEGER NOT NULL ,name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL ,countryCode VARCHAR(3) NOT NULL ,CONSTRAINT States_PK PRIMARY KEY (id));
ALTER TABLE States ADD CONSTRAINT States_UK UNIQUE (countryCode,name);
ALTER TABLE States ADD CONSTRAINT States_country_FK FOREIGN KEY (countryCode) REFERENCES Countries (iso3);

After adding a property phone to Customers and renaming the column icon to icon_name (with previousMapping: icon), a push generates only those changes:

ALTER TABLE customers ADD phone VARCHAR(32);
ALTER TABLE categories RENAME COLUMN icon TO icon_name;

docs.title: Generate the DDL without applying it
docs.text:
With -o, push generates the DDL but does not apply it.

  • -o alone prints the sentences of each source.
  • -o <dir> writes one script per source that changes, named <stage>.<source>.sql. Sources without changes get no file, and a database in step with the model gives no files at all.
lambdaorm push -s default -o migrations

migrations
├── default.catalog.sql
└── default.accounts.sql

The names are deterministic, so the scripts can be renamed into versioned migrations and applied by your own deploy process.

docs.title: Files in orm_state
docs.text:
When push applies the changes, it records them in the orm_state folder:

├── orm_state
│   ├── default-model.json
│   └── main
│       └── V231122154351__push.sql
  • <stage>-model.json: the model of the stage at the last push.
  • <source>/V<yyMMddHHmmss>__push.sql: the sentences executed on that source.

Labs:

  • Simple
  • Two stages
  • Northwind
  • Northwind multiple datasources
  • Northwind CQRS

docs.title: Node
docs.text:
orm.stage.push() returns an action that can give the sentences without applying them, or apply them:

import { Orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib'
(async () => {
    const orm = new Orm()
    try {
        await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml')
        // the sentences, without applying them
        const sentences = await orm.stage.push({ stage: 'default' }).sentence()
        // the sentences grouped by source: [{ source: 'accounts', sentences: ['ALTER TABLE accounts ADD phone VARCHAR(32)'] }]
        const bySource = await orm.stage.push({ stage: 'default' }).sentencesBySource()
        // apply them
        await orm.stage.push({ stage: 'default' }).execute()
    } finally {
        await orm.end()
    }
})()

docs.title: Synchronization
docs.text:
This page summarizes the commands that keep the schema and the databases of a stage in step.

Synchronization works in both directions: from the schema to the sources (databases), and from the sources to the schema file. Each operation is available as a command of the CLI (@lambdaorm/cli) and as a method of orm.stage in @lambdaorm/lib.

Operation Direction Changes the schema Changes the databases push schema → databases no yes pull databases → schema yes no fetch compares both no no introspect data file → schema → databases yes yes incorporate data file → schema → databases, then imports the data yes yes

docs.title: Push
docs.text:
Push updates the sources (databases) with the schema, with the command lambdaorm push.

Push compares the model with the databases themselves: it creates missing tables, adds and alters columns, renames the columns declared with previousMapping, and never drops what exists only in the database. lambdaorm push -o <dir> writes the DDL as one script per source (<stage>.<source>.sql) without applying it.

More information

docs.title: Pull
docs.text:
Pull updates the schema with the structure of the sources (databases), with the command lambdaorm pull. What was written by hand in the schema (relations, listeners, stages) is kept.

More information

docs.title: Fetch
docs.text:
Fetch shows the differences between the sources and the schema, without applying any change, with the command lambdaorm fetch. The result is empty when the databases are in step with the model, and the command exits with code 1 when there are differences (useful in CI).

More information

docs.title: Introspect
docs.text:
Introspect updates the schema from the structure of a JSON data file and then pushes the changes to the sources (databases), with the command lambdaorm introspect.

More information

docs.title: Incorporate
docs.text:
Incorporate does the same as introspect and then imports the data of the file into the sources (databases), with the command lambdaorm incorporate.

docs.title: stackTraceLimit
docs.text:
static stackTraceLimit: number

Defined in: node_modules/.pnpm/@types+node@22.15.29/node_modules/@types/node/globals.d.ts:161

The Error.stackTraceLimit property specifies the number of stack frames collected by a stack trace (whether generated by new Error().stack or Error.captureStackTrace(obj)).

The default value is 10 but may be set to any valid JavaScript number. Changes will affect any stack trace captured after the value has been changed.

If set to a non-number value, or set to a negative number, stack traces will not capture any frames.

docs.title: captureStackTrace()
docs.text:
static captureStackTrace(targetObject, constructorOpt?): void

Defined in: node_modules/.pnpm/@types+node@22.15.29/node_modules/@types/node/globals.d.ts:145

Creates a .stack property on targetObject, which when accessed returns a string representing the location in the code at which Error.captureStackTrace() was called.

const myObject = {};
Error.captureStackTrace(myObject);
myObject.stack;  // Similar to `new Error().stack`

The first line of the trace will be prefixed with ${myObject.name}: ${myObject.message}.

The optional constructorOpt argument accepts a function. If given, all frames above constructorOpt, including constructorOpt, will be omitted from the generated stack trace.

The constructorOpt argument is useful for hiding implementation details of error generation from the user. For instance:

function a() {
  b();
}

function b() {
  c();
}

function c() {
  // Create an error without stack trace to avoid calculating the stack trace twice.
  const { stackTraceLimit } = Error;
  Error.stackTraceLimit = 0;
  const error = new Error();
  Error.stackTraceLimit = stackTraceLimit;

  // Capture the stack trace above function b
  Error.captureStackTrace(error, b); // Neither function c, nor b is included in the stack trace
  throw error;
}

a();

transaction(options, callback): Promise\<void>

Defined in: packages/lib/src/lib/execution/application/services/executor.ts:110

Create a transaction: commit when the callback ends, rollback (and rethrow its error) when it fails. Inside a transaction in course, the callback joins it: the outer transaction commits or rolls back. A transaction can run on several stages (an execution with another stage joins it too); all of them share the connections, one per source, and commit or roll back together.

Defined in: node_modules/.pnpm/@types+node@22.15.29/node_modules/@types/node/globals.d.ts:161

The Error.stackTraceLimit property specifies the number of stack frames collected by a stack trace (whether generated by new Error().stack or Error.captureStackTrace(obj)).

The default value is 10 but may be set to any valid JavaScript number. Changes will affect any stack trace captured after the value has been changed.

If set to a non-number value, or set to a negative number, stack traces will not capture any frames.

docs.title: captureStackTrace()
docs.text:
static captureStackTrace(targetObject, constructorOpt?): void

Defined in: node_modules/.pnpm/@types+node@22.15.29/node_modules/@types/node/globals.d.ts:145

Creates a .stack property on targetObject, which when accessed returns a string representing the location in the code at which Error.captureStackTrace() was called.

const myObject = {};
Error.captureStackTrace(myObject);
myObject.stack;  // Similar to `new Error().stack`

The first line of the trace will be prefixed with ${myObject.name}: ${myObject.message}.

The optional constructorOpt argument accepts a function. If given, all frames above constructorOpt, including constructorOpt, will be omitted from the generated stack trace.

The constructorOpt argument is useful for hiding implementation details of error generation from the user. For instance:

function a() {
  b();
}

function b() {
  c();
}

function c() {
  // Create an error without stack trace to avoid calculating the stack trace twice.
  const { stackTraceLimit } = Error;
  Error.stackTraceLimit = 0;
  const error = new Error();
  Error.stackTraceLimit = stackTraceLimit;

  // Capture the stack trace above function b
  Error.captureStackTrace(error, b); // Neither function c, nor b is included in the stack trace
  throw error;
}

a();

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• e4ce3af: 3xpr 5.2.0 in every package (one copy of it). lib builds each Orm's 3xpr instance with the ExpressionsBuilder 3xpr now exports, instead of importing it from one of its files.
  • Updated dependencies [e4ce3af]
  • @lambdaorm/base@3.2.1

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• 2dc1ac1: Fixes found running the same checks on every engine (engines lab, docs/PLAN.md B7):

  • stage.fetch / push compare a column the way the dialect creates it: no false drift (and no needless ALTER) for MySQL/MariaDB booleans, Oracle numbers and nullability, SQL Server and MariaDB json; MariaDB LONGTEXT is read.

  • MySQL/MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle: in(p.x, list) with the list in a variable.
  • json columns are read as objects also where the driver answers text (MariaDB, Oracle CLOB); SQL Server writes them.
  • SQL Server: delete with a filter (DELETE c FROM t c).
  • Oracle: autoIncrement columns are identity columns; booleans are written as Y/N.
  • MongoDB: transactions commit and roll back (the session was not used), update/delete answer the matched/deleted documents, autoIncrement keys, string literals and '' in filters, json values, in with a list, include of a composite relation, and update().include() of a composite saves the embedded children.

  • upsert on SQL Server, Oracle and MongoDB says it is not supported yet.

  • 68faedb: Each Orm has its own 3xpr instance. With the shared one, every new Orm() replaced orm.execute (and the other orm.* functions): the listeners and scripts of an earlier Orm ran their queries on the last one created, outside their own transaction.

docs.title: Minor Changes
docs.text:
• 7c18bef: - A filter by a field of a relation whose entity lives in another source works (L15): QuoteLines.filter(p => p.deviceModel.name == name) first queries DeviceModels on its source and then filters QuoteLines with in(p.deviceModelId, …). Each comparison is solved on its own (&&, ||, ! keep their meaning); the other side must be a value (a clear error otherwise) and only one level of relation is supported.
  • PostgreSQL: in(p.x, list) / p.x.in(list) with the list in a variable works — the parameter was typed as its elements and the array was sent as a Postgres array literal (L33).
  • 38e7d3b: New orm.executeScript(script, data, options): evaluates a 3xpr script whose orm.execute(query, data, options) calls all run in one transaction, also across sources. The script can use variables, if, for, for … in, throw, try/catch and return; it commits when it ends and rolls back and rejects when anything fails (a query, a function or a throw). It works on a copy of data, cannot read environment variables, and its orm.execute calls without a stage run on the script's stage. Returns the value of the last statement (or of return).
const quoteId = await orm.executeScript(
  `
  orm.execute("Quotes.insert()", { id: quoteId, accountId: accountId, status: "draft" });
  for (line in lines) {
    orm.execute("QuoteLines.insert()", { id: line.id, quoteId: quoteId, deviceModelId: line.modelId, quantity: line.qty });
  }
  orm.execute("Accounts.update(p => ({ lastQuoteAt: now() })).filter(p => p.id == accountId)", { accountId: accountId });
  quoteId
`,
  { quoteId, accountId, lines }
);
  • 3f3e1cc: Listeners (application.listeners) are awaited one after the other and run in the sentence's transaction: their orm.execute calls use the same connections, an error in before prevents the sentence, an error in after fails it, and a rollback undoes what they wrote. A sentence with listeners that runs on its own opens a transaction for itself and its listeners. They used to run detached (forEach(async …)): execute could return before them, their errors escaped as uncaught exceptions and they wrote outside the transaction — L10.

New listener option transactional: false (base ListenerConfig): the listener runs outside the transaction, and what it writes is kept even if the sentence's transaction rolls back.

  • c2be59f: push compares the model with the databases (as fetch reads them), not with orm_state — L19: a new environment or a CI runner without the last push's orm_state no longer gets CREATE TABLE for tables that exist. Tables missing in the database are created with their keys, FKs and indexes; in existing tables, missing columns are added (ADD COLUMN, L27), columns with another type, length or nullability are altered, and a property mapping with previousMapping: <old column> renames the column (ALTER TABLE … RENAME COLUMN, L20; SqlServer sp_rename). Nothing that exists only in the database is dropped (stage.fetch() reports it). orm_state is still written by push as a record.
  • d16b60a: stage.push().sentencesBySource(): the DDL grouped per source (one script per database). cli: lambdaorm push -o <dir> writes one script per source that changes, <stage>.<source>.sql (deterministic names, to rename into a versioned migration); -o without a folder prints the DDL grouped by source — L19.
  • e961817: update().include(p => p.children) on a composite relation saves the aggregate: the children sent are inserted or updated (upsert by primary key, with the parent's key), and the parent's children that were not sent are deleted. Children absent from the data are not touched. It used to update only the existing children that were sent — L17. Supported where upsert is (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB); SqlServer, Oracle and SQLjs report it as not supported yet (MongoDB keeps composite children embedded). An explicit include(p => p.children.update(…)) keeps updating only.

  • 8b8f470: Stage commands:

  • push/DDL: a stage's last source without condition is a catch-all, as in DML: it gets only the entities no other source took (it used to receive every entity) — L25.

  • fetch/pull on PostgreSQL work with reserved words as column names (order): the metadata query quoted the column twice — L6, L21.
  • stage.fetch() reports the drift: per mapping, the entities that differ from the model (present in one side only, different columns, types, lengths, required, primary key), each with its differences; no entities when in step. stage.read() returns the databases' mappings as fetch did (pull uses it) — L22.

  • cli: lambdaorm fetch exits with code 1 when there are differences (for CI). fetch, pull, schema, introspect and incorporate load the --envfile they declared (it was ignored).

  • 907074b: Transactions:

  • orm.transaction now waits for the transaction: it resolves after the commit and rejects with the callback's error after the rollback (the error used to escape as an uncaught exception and the promise resolved undefined) — L26. If the rollback itself fails, the callback's error is still the one reported.

  • Everything executed inside orm.transaction joins it, also when it doesn't go through tr: orm.execute, repositories, the orm.execute function of an expression. It runs on the transaction's connections (one per source), so a rollback undoes it — L31. A nested orm.transaction joins the outer one, a query with include no longer opens a second transaction, and an execution on another stage inside a transaction fails with a clear error. Each Orm instance keeps its own transaction context.

  • 7c8edd7: Types and values:

  • New property type json (L1): objects and lists are written as JSON and come back as objects and lists. Column type: PostgreSQL JSONB, MySQL/MariaDB JSON, SqlServer NVARCHAR(MAX), Oracle CLOB, others TEXT. A list is no longer sent as a Postgres array literal.

  • The mapping's dbType reaches the DDL when a table or column is created or altered (it was used in one place only) — e.g. dbType: timestamptz(3) (L1, L2).
  • PostgreSQL writes dateTime with milliseconds and the offset (yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSSZZ): milliseconds are kept and a timestamptz column stores the exact instant; timestamp columns keep storing the local time (L2).
  • '', 0 and false parameters are values: only undefined becomes NULL (an empty string used to be written as NULL, and so were 0 and false) — L3. (The "" literal needs 3xpr 5.1.1.)

  • A string property without length is no longer given length 80 in the model: PostgreSQL creates TEXT, the other dialects keep VARCHAR(80) — L24. On PostgreSQL, the next push of an existing model widens those columns to TEXT.

  • de140f3: update answers the number of affected rows (as delete does, and as the repositories' update(): Promise<number> always declared); it answered { data: <parameters> }. Lets callers detect "not found" (0) and optimistic-lock conflicts (filter(p => p.id == id && p.version == version) → 0) — L4. SQLjs update/delete now return the modified rows too.

  • 6319468: Entity.upsert(): insert, or update the row with the same primary key, in one sentence — PostgreSQL INSERT … ON CONFLICT (pk) DO UPDATE SET c = EXCLUDED.c, MySQL/MariaDB ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE c = VALUES(c) (other dialects: a clear "not supported" error). Written like an insert (upsert(), upsert(entity), upsert({ … })); answers the data like insert — L18. It used to fail with function: upsert not found.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• 2ee8930: Upgrade the data7expressions dependencies to their latest major: 3xpr from 1.x to ^5.1.1, h3lp and typ3s to ^5.0.0 (and json-light to ^5.0.0 in the CLI). No API changes were needed. Behaviour inherited from 3xpr:

  • <= now has the same precedence as the other comparison operators (a <= b == true used to evaluate as a <= (b == true)).

  • 3xpr 5.1.0 evaluates async expressions statement by statement (listeners, orm.execute inside expressions), never runs an async function while building an expression, and adds throw, try/catch, return, break and continue; 3xpr 5.1.1 parses the empty string literal "" (it used to swallow the rest of the expression).

  • ee1e7ac: Packaging:

  • The published exports pointed to ./build/lib/index.js, a path the package doesn't have: require('@lambdaorm/lib') (and base, client) failed for everyone installing from npm. dist now rewrites exports (and bin) like main — L7.

  • cli: declares bin: lambdaorm, so npm i -g @lambdaorm/cli installs the lambdaorm command — L29.

  • Every package's dist is smoke-tested before it can be released: required by its name (so exports applies) and, for the CLI, lambdaorm --help.

  • b1dcd8b: - orm.executeScript(script, data, options, { timeout }): when the timeout passes the script's transaction rolls back and the promise rejects.

  • A finished transaction (committed or rolled back) refuses any later execution, so work that outlives it (a script that timed out, a kept tr) never reaches the database.
  • ExecutionError keeps the database's error code (error.code, e.g. Postgres 23505); it used to be lost.

docs.title: Repositories
docs.text: A repository is associated with an entity and has methods to query and modify it, without writing the whole query.

docs.title: Generating repositories
docs.text:
The lambdaorm build command generates the model (model.ts) and one repository per entity (repository<Entity>.ts) in the domain path of the project:

lambdaorm build -w lab/northwind -r

A repository file is generated only if it does not exist yet, so it is safe to add custom methods to it.

import { Repository, IOrm } from '@lambdaorm/lib'
import { Product, QryProduct } from './model'

export class ProductRepository extends Repository<Product, QryProduct> {
  constructor (stage?: string, orm?: IOrm) {
    super('Products', stage, orm)
  }
  // Add your code here
}

The constructor receives the stage (optional: the default stage when omitted) and, optionally, the orm instance.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib'
import { ProductRepository } from './northwind/domain/repositoryProduct'

(async () => {
  await orm.init()
  const productRepository = new ProductRepository('default')
  const country = 'USA'
  const result = await productRepository.query()
    .filter(p => (p.price > 5 && p.supplier.country == country) || (p.inStock < 3))
    .having(p => max(p.price) > 50)
    .map(p => ({ category: p.category.name, largestPrice: max(p.price) }))
    .sort(p => desc(p.largestPrice))
    .execute({ country })
  console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2))
  await orm.end()
})()

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method Description insert(entity, include?) Inserts a record (and, with include, its related records). bulkInsert(entities, include?) Inserts several records. update(entity, include?) Updates a record. updateAll(data, map, filter?, include?) Updates all the records that match the filter (or all the records of the entity). upsert(entity, include?) Inserts a record, or updates it if one with the same primary key exists (upsert). bulkMerge(entities, include?) Inserts or updates several records. delete(entity, include?) Deletes a record. bulkDelete(entities, include?) Deletes several records. deleteAll(data, filter?, include?) Deletes all the records that match the filter (or all the records of the entity). list(data, filter?, include?) Returns the records that match the filter. distinct(data, filter?, include?) Returns the distinct records that match the filter. first(data, filter?, include?) Returns the first record, or null. last(data, filter?, include?) Returns the last record, or null. query() Starts a custom query on the entity (filter, include, having, map, sort, page, …), run with execute(data). execute(query, data?) Runs a query string appended to the entity, for example .filter(p => p.id == id).

data holds the values of the parameters used by filter and map.

docs.title: Script
docs.text: A script is a small program, written in 3xpr (a JavaScript-like expression language), that λORM runs with orm.executeScript(script, data, options). Inside it, orm.execute(query, data, options) runs λORM queries, and variables, conditions and loops decide which ones and with what data.

docs.title: What it is for
docs.text:
Many use cases are more than one query: place an order (the order, its lines, the customer's balance), move stock between warehouses, register a payment and its audit. Their writes must happen completely or not at all: an order without its lines, or a balance discounted for an order that was not saved, is a corrupt state.

orm.transaction(options, callback) solves it in Node.js code. A script solves it in a single call that carries the whole use case, wherever the call comes from: Node.js (orm.executeScript), the Data Gateway (POST /script), the Node.js client (@lambdaorm/client) or the CLI (lambdaorm script). A client in any language can run a use case with several reads and writes in one transaction, which it could not do by sending one query per request.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• All or nothing: everything the script executes is one transaction — committed when it ends, rolled back if anything fails (a query, a throw, the timeout). See below.
  • Across sources and stages: queries on several databases, and on another stage with orm.execute(query, data, { stage: "insights" }), are part of the same transaction.
  • Listeners included: what the schema's listeners write is committed or undone with the script.
  • A language, not only queries: variables, if, for, while, switch, try/catch, throw, return, list functions (filter, map, sum, …) and every function of 3xpr and λORM.
  • Read your writes: a statement sees what the previous ones wrote, before the commit.
  • A result: the value of the last statement (or of return) — a value, a row, an object built by the script.
  • Safe for scripts sent by clients: no access to environment variables, works on a copy of data, timeout and maxIterations stop it (also a loop that never ends), and the Data Gateway runs scripts only when its configuration enables them (scripts.enabled) and the credential has the script permission.

A first look — the examples go step by step, from a single query to a complete use case:

const total = await orm.executeScript(`
  orm.execute("Orders.insert()", { id: orderId, status: "new", version: 1 });
  for (l in lines) {
    orm.execute("OrderLines.insert()", {
      orderId:  orderId,
      line:     l.line,
      product:  l.product,
      quantity: l.qty
    });
  }
  lines.sum(p => p.qty * p.price)
`,
  { orderId, lines },
  { stage: 'default' }
)

docs.title: The main feature: all or nothing
docs.text:
Everything a script executes is one transaction. Every orm.execute of the script — on one source or on several, on the script's stage or on another one, and what the listeners write — runs on the same connections:

  • when the script ends, everything is committed;
  • if anything fails — a query, a function, a rule that throws, the timeout — everything the script did is rolled back, in every source and stage, and the promise rejects with that error.

That is what a script is for: a use case with several reads and writes (an order with its lines, a stock movement, a transfer) that must happen completely or not at all, in a single call — also from the Data Gateway (POST /script), the client or the CLI, where a client could otherwise only send one query per request and could not undo the previous ones.

When the script… Result ends normally commit of everything; resolves with the last value (or return) throws (throw) rollback of everything; rejects with that error runs a query that fails (e.g. a duplicate key) rollback of everything; rejects with the database's error catches an error with try/catch it goes on; the error does not undo anything by itself passes timeout or maxIterations it stops, rollback of everything; rejects

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
Argument Description script The 3xpr script data The variables of the script. The script works on a copy: data is never changed options The query options plus the script's limits (ScriptOptions), see below Option Description stage The stage of the transaction and of every orm.execute without a stage timeout Max time in ms: when it passes, the loops stop, the transaction rolls back and the script rejects maxIterations Max loop iterations of the script, all loops together; past it the script fails and rolls back

Up to @lambdaorm/lib 3.3.0 the limits were a fourth argument (executeScript(script, data, options, { timeout, maxIterations })); since 3.4.0 everything goes in options.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Each example says what it does and what happens when it fails.

docs.title: The model of the examples
docs.text:
domain:
  entities:
    - name: Customers
      primaryKey: [id]
      uniqueKey: [code]
      properties:
        - { name: id, type: integer, required: true, autoIncrement: true }
        - { name: code, length: 20, required: true }
        - { name: name, required: true }
        - { name: notes }
        - { name: balance, type: decimal }
    - name: Orders
      primaryKey: [id]
      properties:
        - { name: id, length: 36, required: true }
        - { name: customerId, type: integer }
        - { name: status, length: 20, required: true }
        - { name: version, type: integer, required: true }
      relations:
        - { name: lines, type: manyToOne, composite: true, from: id, entity: OrderLines, to: orderId }
    - name: OrderLines
      primaryKey: [orderId, line]
      properties:
        - { name: orderId, length: 36, required: true }
        - { name: line, type: integer, required: true }
        - { name: product, length: 40, required: true }
        - { name: quantity, type: integer }
    - name: AuditLogs
      primaryKey: [id]
      properties:
        - { name: id, type: integer, required: true, autoIncrement: true }
        - { name: entityName, length: 40 }
        - { name: refId, length: 36 }

The examples run on the stage default; examples 11 and 13 also write on a stage insights. They are the engines lab model, where the same scripts are tested on PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle and MongoDB.

docs.title: 1. A single query
docs.text:
The simplest script is one orm.execute. The script returns the value of its last statement — here the rows of the query. Even this runs in a transaction (it opens, the query runs, it commits).

const result = await orm.executeScript(`
  orm.execute("Customers.filter(p => p.code == code)", { code: code })
`,
  { code },
  { stage: 'default' }
)

docs.title: 2. Several statements, in order
docs.text:
Statements run one after the other, each orm.execute awaited before the next. A statement sees what the previous ones wrote, before the commit (they share the connection).

const result = await orm.executeScript(`
  orm.execute("Customers.insert()", { code: code, name: name });
  orm.execute("Customers.filter(p => p.code == code).map(p => p.name)", { code: code })
`,
  { code, name: 'Ana' },
  { stage: 'default' }
)

Result: [{ name: "Ana" }].

docs.title: 3. Using the result of a statement
docs.text:
Assign a result to a variable and use it below. An insert answers { data } with the values written, generated ones included: customer.data.id is the id the database generated.

const result = await orm.executeScript(`
  customer = orm.execute("Customers.insert()", { code: code, name: name });
  orm.execute("Orders.insert()", { id: orderId, customerId: customer.data.id, status: "new", version: 1 });
  customer.data.id
`,
  { code, name: 'Ana', orderId },
  { stage: 'default' }
)

Result: the id generated for the customer.

docs.title: 4. Affected rows: "not found" as an error
docs.text:
update and delete answer the number of affected rows. A script can turn 0 into an error; throw with a status is answered with that HTTP status by the Data Gateway.

const result = await orm.executeScript(`
  updated = orm.execute("Customers.update(p => ({ name: name })).filter(p => p.code == code)", { code: code, name: name });
  if (updated == 0) {
    throw { status: 404, message: "customer " + code + " not found" };
  }
  updated
`,
  { code: 'missing', name: 'Bob' },
  { stage: 'default' }
)

Result: rejects: customer missing not found (404).

docs.title: 5. Conditions: create only what is missing
docs.text:
if with a query in the condition. Run it twice with the same data: the second time it creates nothing.

const result = await orm.executeScript(`
  created = 0;
  for (c in customers) {
    if (orm.execute("Customers.filter(p => p.code == code)", { code: c.code }).length() == 0) {
      orm.execute("Customers.insert()", c);
      created += 1;
    }
  }
  created
`,
  { customers: [{ code: 'c1', name: 'Ana' }, { code: 'c2', name: 'Bob' }] },
  { stage: 'default' }
)

Result: 2 the first time, 0 the second.

docs.title: 6. Loops: one row per item
docs.text:
for (item in list) over the data. Every insert of the loop is in the same transaction: all the lines are written, or none. Lists also have filter, map, sum, count…

const result = await orm.executeScript(`
  orm.execute("Orders.insert()", { id: orderId, status: "new", version: 1 });
  for (l in lines) {
    orm.execute("OrderLines.insert()", { orderId: orderId, line: l.line, product: l.product, quantity: l.qty });
  }
  lines.sum(p => p.qty * p.price)
`,
  { orderId, lines: [{ line: 1, product: 'camera', qty: 2, price: 10 }, { line: 2, product: 'hub', qty: 1, price: 5 }] },
  { stage: 'default' }
)

Result: 25.

docs.title: 7. Aggregates with include
docs.text:
A composite relation can be written with include, as in orm.execute outside a script. Here the order and its lines in one sentence, then read back with its lines.

const result = await orm.executeScript(`
  orm.execute("Orders.insert().include(p => p.lines)", {
    id: orderId, status: "new", version: 1,
    lines: lines.map(l => ({ orderId: orderId, line: l.line, product: l.product, quantity: l.qty }))
  });
  orders = orm.execute("Orders.filter(p => p.id == orderId).include(p => p.lines)", { orderId: orderId });
  orders[0].lines.length()
`,
  { orderId, lines: [{ line: 1, product: 'camera', qty: 2 }, { line: 2, product: 'hub', qty: 1 }] },
  { stage: 'default' }
)

Result: 2.

docs.title: 8. A business rule: throw, and everything is undone
docs.text:
The rule is checked after writing: the order and its lines are already in the database (inside the transaction). throw stops the script and rolls back everything it wrote: no order and no line is left.

const result = await orm.executeScript(`
  orm.execute("Orders.insert()", { id: orderId, status: "new", version: 1 });
  for (l in lines) {
    orm.execute("OrderLines.insert()", { orderId: orderId, line: l.line, product: l.product, quantity: l.qty });
  }
  total = lines.sum(p => p.qty * p.price);
  if (total > maxTotal) {
    throw { status: 400, message: "the order exceeds " + maxTotal };
  }
  total
`,
  { orderId, maxTotal: 20, lines: [ …total 25… ] },
  { stage: 'default' }
)

Result: rejects: the order exceeds 20 (400); the order and its lines are not in the database.

docs.title: 9. Handling an error: try / catch
docs.text:
An error caught with try/catch does not abort the script: it goes on and commits. Use it for optional steps; any error not caught rolls everything back.

const result = await orm.executeScript(`
  try {
    if (vip) { throw "vip customers are reviewed by hand"; }
    note = "ok";
  } catch (e) {
    note = e.message;
  }
  orm.execute("Customers.insert()", { code: code, name: name, notes: note });
  note
`,
  { code, name: 'Ana', vip: true },
  { stage: 'default' }
)

Result: "vip customers are reviewed by hand" (and the customer is written).

docs.title: 10. Listeners run inside the script's transaction
docs.text:
A schema listener (here, one that writes an AuditLogs row after each order insert) runs in the script's transaction: committed with it, and undone with it if the script fails.

application:
  listeners:
    - name: auditOrders
      on: [insert]
      condition: entity == "Orders"
      after: orm.execute("AuditLogs.insert()", { entityName: "Orders", refId: data.id })

const result = await orm.executeScript(`
  orm.execute("Orders.insert()", { id: orderId, status: "new", version: 1 });
  throw "cancel";
`,
  { orderId },
  { stage: 'default' }
)

Result: rejects: cancel; neither the order nor its audit row are in the database.

docs.title: 11. Another stage in the same transaction
docs.text:
orm.execute(query, data, { stage: "insights" }) runs on another stage — other sources, even another database engine — in the same transaction: if anything fails afterwards, the write on the other stage is undone too.

const result = await orm.executeScript(`
  orm.execute("Orders.insert()", { id: orderId, status: "new", version: 1 });
  orm.execute("AuditLogs.insert()", { entityName: "new order", refId: orderId }, { stage: insights });
  if (fail) { throw "something failed after both writes"; }
  "done"
`,
  { orderId, insights: 'insights', fail: true },
  { stage: 'default' }
)

Result: rejects; the order (default stage) and the audit row (insights stage) are both undone.

docs.title: 12. Limits: timeout and maxIterations
docs.text:
Options of the script, with the stage: timeout (ms) stops it — also a loop that never ends — and rolls back; maxIterations caps the loop iterations of the whole script. Both are worth setting when scripts come from clients.

const result = await orm.executeScript(`
  orm.execute("Customers.insert()", { code: code, name: "never kept" });
  while (true) { x = 1; }
`,
  { code },
  { stage: 'default', timeout: 2000, maxIterations: 10000 }
)

Result: rejects (maxIterations, or the timeout first); the customer is not written.

docs.title: 13. A complete use case: place an order
docs.text:
Everything together: validate, write an aggregate, apply a rule, write on another stage and answer a summary. One call, one transaction — if any step fails, nothing of the order exists anywhere.

const result = await orm.executeScript(`
  customers = orm.execute("Customers.filter(p => p.code == customerCode)", { customerCode: customerCode });
  if (customers.length() == 0) {
    throw { status: 404, message: "customer " + customerCode + " not found" };
  }
  customer = customers[0];

  orm.execute("Orders.insert()", { id: orderId, customerId: customer.id, status: "new", version: 1 });

  for (l in lines) {
    orm.execute("OrderLines.insert()", {
      orderId:  orderId,
      line:     l.line,
      product:  l.product,
      quantity: l.qty
    });
  }

  total = lines.sum(p => p.qty * p.price);
  if (total > customer.balance) {
    throw { status: 409, message: "insufficient balance" };
  }

  orm.execute("Customers.update(p => ({ balance: balance })).filter(p => p.id == id)", {
    id:      customer.id,
    balance: customer.balance - total
  });
  orm.execute("AuditLogs.insert()", { entityName: "order total " + total, refId: orderId }, { stage: insights });

  { orderId: orderId, total: total, balance: customer.balance - total }
`,
  { customerCode: 'c1', orderId, insights: 'insights', lines: [{ line: 1, product: 'camera', qty: 2, price: 10 }, { line: 2, product: 'hub', qty: 1, price: 5 }] },
  { stage: 'default', timeout: 10000, maxIterations: 10000 }
)

Result: { orderId, total: 25, balance: 75 } with a balance of 100; with a balance of 20 it rejects (409) and the order, its lines, the balance and the audit row are left as they were.

docs.title: 14. Another use case: a quote with its total on insights
docs.text:
A quote with its lines on the main stage and its total on the insights stage (other sources, possibly another database), in one transaction. The account must exist; if any step fails, neither the quote, nor its lines, nor the total are left anywhere. (A model with Accounts, Quotes, QuoteLines and QuoteTotals.)

const quoteId = await orm.executeScript(`
  account = orm.execute("Accounts.filter(p => p.id == accountId)", { accountId: accountId });
  if (account.length() == 0) {
    throw { status: 404, message: "account not found" };
  }

  orm.execute("Quotes.insert()", { id: quoteId, accountId: accountId, status: "draft" });

  for (line in lines) {
    orm.execute("QuoteLines.insert()", {
      id:        line.id,
      quoteId:   quoteId,
      productId: line.productId,
      quantity:  line.qty
    });
  }

  total = lines.sum(p => p.qty * p.price);
  orm.execute("QuoteTotals.insert()", { quoteId: quoteId, total: total }, { stage: "insights" });

  quoteId
`,
  { quoteId, accountId, lines },
  { stage: 'default', timeout: 10000, maxIterations: 10000 }
)

docs.title: The same script from a client
docs.text:
The script and its data are the same everywhere; only the call changes. The URL of the Data Gateway includes the route of the schema, unless the gateway serves a single schema at the root, as in these examples.

// @lambdaorm/client, against a Data Gateway
import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/client'
await orm.init('http://localhost:8080', { headers: { 'X-Api-Key': process.env.BACKEND_KEY } })
const result = await orm.executeScript(script, data, { stage: 'default', timeout: 10000 })

# REST: a Data Gateway with scripts.enabled and a credential with the script permission
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/script -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H "X-Api-Key: $BACKEND_KEY" \
  -d '{ "script": "orm.execute(\"Customers.filter(p => p.code == code)\", { code: code })", "data": { "code": "c1" }, "options": { "stage": "default" } }'

# CLI: a script file, data as JSON
lambdaorm script -f place-order.3xpr -d '{ "customerCode": "c1", "orderId": "o-1", "lines": [] }' -s default

docs.title: The language
docs.text:
Everything 3xpr has:

  • Variables: total = 0;, objects { id: id, name: "x" }, lists [1, 2], items[0].name.
  • if / else if / else, while, for (i = 0; i < n; i += 1), for (item in items), switch/case, break, continue, return.
  • throw "message"; try { … } catch (e) { e.message }. throw { status: 404, message: "…" } makes the Data Gateway answer with that status; in Node the error's message is that object as JSON.
  • Arrow functions as arguments: items.filter(p => p.qty > 1).map(p => p.name), items.sum(p => p.qty), items.each(p => …).
  • 3xpr's functions: strings (upper, concat, …), numbers, dates (now(), …), lists, nvl, iif, … (see Operators & Functions).
  • Not available: the ? : operator (iif(c, a, b) evaluates both sides), ++/-- (use i += 1) and declaring functions.

Statements run in order, and each orm.execute is awaited before the next statement.

Plus the functions λORM adds:

Function Description orm.execute(query, data, options) Executes a query in the script's transaction; options.stage may name another stage (same transaction) orm.plan(query, options) The plan of a query (.sentence, …) orm.parameters(query) The parameters of a query orm.metadata(query) The metadata of a query orm.model(query) The model (fields) a query returns orm.constraints(query) The constraints a query checks toBase64(value) / getBase64(value) "abc" → "YWJj" and back encrypt(value, key) / decrypt(value, key) AES

docs.title: Writing scripts: a few rules
docs.text:
• Statements end with ;; the last one (without ;) is the result. return value; ends the script early.
  • Variables need no declaration: total = 0;. data is copied: the script never changes the caller's object.
  • Count with i += 1 (there is no ++); use iif(condition, a, b) (there is no ? :).
  • A query's result can be indexed directly: orm.execute("Customers.filter(p => p.code == code)", { code: code })[0].name; an empty list is [] (both need 3xpr 5.3.1, from @lambdaorm/lib 3.4.1).
  • A script can't read environment variables ($VAR).

docs.title: Transaction and stages
docs.text:
• One transaction for the whole script, also across sources and stages: commit at the end; rollback and reject on any error.
  • orm.execute(query, data) without stage runs on the stage of options; with { stage: "insights" } it runs on that stage, in the same transaction (since @lambdaorm/lib 3.3.0).
  • A statement sees what the previous ones wrote (same connection), before the commit.
  • There is no two-phase commit: with several databases the commit goes source by source.

docs.title: Security and limits
docs.text:
• The script cannot read environment variables ($VAR fails), so it can't read connection strings.
  • timeout: when it passes, the script's loops stop, the transaction rolls back and the script rejects; whatever it still executes afterwards fails without reaching the database.
  • maxIterations: the loop iterations of the script, all loops together; past it the script fails and rolls back. The Data Gateway uses scripts.maxIterations (default 100000).
  • Since @lambdaorm/lib 3.3.0 (3xpr 5.3.0) a while (true) {} no longer blocks the process: the timeout and maxIterations stop it. In the Data Gateway scripts are off by default (scripts.enabled) and need the script permission.

docs.title: Script examples
docs.text: The examples are now in the Script page.

docs.title: Transaction
docs.text: A transaction groups several executions so that they are all committed together or all rolled back. In λORM a transaction is opened with orm.transaction(options, callback).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
orm.transaction receives:

  • options: the query options, for example the stage ({ stage: 'default' });
  • callback: an async function that receives a transaction object (named tr in the examples) and executes the queries with tr.execute(query, data, options).

When the callback ends, λORM commits; if it throws, λORM rolls back.

await orm.transaction({ stage: 'default' }, async tr => {
  await tr.execute('Quotes.insert()', quote)
  // orm.execute inside the callback also joins the transaction
  await orm.execute('Accounts.update(p => ({ lastQuoteAt: at })).filter(p => p.id == id)', { id: quote.accountId, at: new Date() })
  // another stage: same transaction
  await tr.execute('QuoteSummaries.insert()', summary, { stage: 'insights' })
})

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
• The promise resolves after the commit and rejects with the callback's error after the rollback. If the rollback itself fails, the callback's error is still the one reported.
  • Everything executed inside the callback joins the transaction: tr.execute, orm.execute, repositories, and the orm.execute of a listener or of an expression. They run on the transaction's connections (one per source), so a rollback undoes them in every source.
  • A nested orm.transaction joins the outer one: there is a single commit, done by the outer transaction.
  • An execution without a stage runs on the transaction's stage. An execution with another stage joins the transaction too (since @lambdaorm/lib 3.3.0): every stage shares the transaction's connections, and they commit or roll back together.
  • A finished transaction rejects later executions.

Warning

There is no two-phase commit: with several databases, the commit is done source by source. If a later commit fails, the earlier ones are kept.

To run several queries in one transaction from a single call — also over the Data Gateway or the CLI — see Script.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The order and its details are inserted, read, updated and deleted in the same transaction:

import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib'
import { Orders } from './northwind/domain/model'

(async () => {
  try {
    await orm.init('./config/northwind.yaml')
    const order = {
      customerId: 'VINET', employeeId: 5, orderDate: '1996-07-03T22:00:00.000Z', requiredDate: '1996-07-31T22:00:00.000Z',
      shippedDate: '1996-07-15T22:00:00.000Z', shipViaId: 3, freight: 32.38, name: 'Vins et alcools Chevalier',
      address: '59 rue de l-Abbaye', city: 'Reims', region: null, postalCode: '51100', country: 'France',
      details: [
        { productId: 11, unitPrice: 14, quantity: 12, discount: false },
        { productId: 42, unitPrice: 9.8, quantity: 10, discount: false },
        { productId: 72, unitPrice: 34.8, quantity: 5, discount: false }
      ]
    }
    await orm.transaction({ stage: 'default' }, async (tr) => {
      // create the order
      const orderId = await tr.execute(() => Orders.insert().include(p => p.details), order)
      // get the order
      const result = await tr.execute((id: number) => Orders.filter(p => p.id === id).include(p => p.details), { id: orderId })
      const order2 = result[0]
      // update the order
      order2.address = 'changed 59 rue de l-Abbaye'
      order2.details[0].discount = true
      order2.details[1].unitPrice = 10
      order2.details[2].quantity = 7
      const updateCount = await tr.execute(() => Orders.update().include(p => p.details), order2)
      console.log(updateCount)
      // get the order again
      const order3 = await tr.execute((id: number) => Orders.filter(p => p.id === id).include(p => p.details), { id: orderId })
      console.log(JSON.stringify(order3))
      // delete the order
      const deleteCount = await tr.execute(() => Orders.delete().include(p => p.details), order3[0])
      console.log(deleteCount)
      // the order no longer exists
      const order4 = await tr.execute((id: number) => Orders.filter(p => p.id === id).include(p => p.details), { id: orderId })
      console.log(JSON.stringify(order4))
    })
  } catch (error: any) {
    console.error(error.stack)
  } finally {
    // close the connections
    await orm.end()
  }
})()

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
This page shows different ways of using λORM with the same example domain (Northwind) on different infrastructures: a single source, several sources, CQRS with several stages, and a Node.js client connected to a Data Gateway.

To keep the schemas short, the properties, keys, indexes and relations of the entities, as well as the mappings, are omitted. The complete schemas are in the labs.

docs.title: Schema
docs.text:
The domain has five entities: Categories, Customers, Products and Orders, where Orders is a composite entity made of the orders and their details (Orders.details). The infrastructure has a single stage with a single source, Ordering, a MySQL database that uses the default mapping.

domain:  
  entities:
  - name: Categories
  - name: Customers
  - name: Products
  - name: Orders
  - name: Orders.details
infrastructure:
  mappings:
  - name: default
  sources:
    - name: Ordering
      mapping: default
      dialect: MySQL
      connection: ${CNN_MYSQL}
  stages:
  - name: default
    sources:
      - name: Ordering

docs.title: Query
docs.text:
The query gets an order of a customer, with its details. It is written as a lambda expression and run with the @lambdaorm/lib library.

import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/lib'
import { Orders } from './northwind/domain/model'

(async () => {
  try {
    // initialize the ORM with the schema file
    await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml')
    // query
    const query = (customerId: string) => Orders
      .filter(p => p.customerId == customerId)
      .include(p => [
        p.customer.map(p => p.name),
        p.details
          .include(p => p.product
            .include(p => p.category.map(p => p.name))
            .map(p => p.name))
          .map(p => [p.quantity, p.unitPrice])
      ])
      .page(1, 1)
    // execute the query
    const result = await orm.execute(query, { customerId: 'CENTC' })
    console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2))
  } catch (error: any) {
    console.error(error)
  } finally {
    await orm.end()
  }
})()

docs.title: Schema
docs.text:
In this case the entities of the domain are stored in different sources:

  • Categories and Products are stored in the Catalog source, a MySQL database that uses the default mapping.
  • Customers is stored in the Crm source, a PostgreSQL database that uses the default mapping.
  • Orders is stored in the Ordering source, a MongoDB database that uses the mongoDb mapping.

The condition of each source in the stage decides which entities it stores.

domain:  
  entities:
  - name: Categories
  - name: Customers
  - name: Products
  - name: Orders
  - name: Orders.details
infrastructure:
  mappings:
  - name: default
  - name: mongoDb
    extends: default
  sources:
  - name: Catalog      
    dialect: MySQL
    mapping: default
    connection: ${CNN_MYSQL}      
  - name: Crm    
    dialect: PostgreSQL
    mapping: default
    connection: ${CNN_POSTGRES}
  - name: Ordering
    dialect: MongoDB
    mapping: mongoDb      
    connection: ${CNN_MONGODB}    
  stages:
  - name: default
    sources:
    - name: Catalog
      condition: entity.in(["Categories","Products"])
    - name: Crm
      condition: entity.in(["Address","Customers"])
    - name: Ordering
      condition: entity.in(["Orders","Orders.details"])

docs.title: Query
docs.text:
This time the query is run from the CLI. The code does not change with the infrastructure, and the result is the same as in the previous case, although the data now comes from three databases.

lambdaorm execute -e ".env" -q "Orders.filter(p => p.customerId == customerId).include(p => [p.customer.map(p => p.name), p.details.include(p => p.product.include(p => p.category.map(p => p.name)).map(p => p.name)).map(p => [p.quantity, p.unitPrice])]).page(1,1)" -d "{\"customerId\": \"CENTC\"}"

    },
